subject: theory
title: Complexity Theory
summary: P, NP and the P vs NP question, NP-completeness and Cook–Levin, worked reductions, coping with NP-hardness, space complexity and PSPACE, and the randomised and quantum classes BPP and BQP, with a clear line between what is proven and what is conjectured.

lessons.title: Decision problems and input cost
lessons.summary: Measure input size in bits, so large values can have short encodings.
lessons.body:
Computability asks whether a problem can be solved by an algorithm at all. **Complexity theory** asks a sharper question: how much time or memory does it take, as the input grows?

The headline result of the field is a question nobody has answered. Is every problem whose solutions are easy to **check** also easy to **solve**? That is the **P vs NP** problem, and this lesson sets up exactly what it means.

## Measuring cost

Three conventions make the theory work.

1. **Decision problems.** We mostly study yes/no questions: "does this graph have a route of length at most 100?" rather than "find the shortest route". A yes/no problem is just a set of inputs (a **formal language**) whose answer is yes.
2. **Input size n is measured in bits.** A positive integer takes roughly its base-two logarithm in bits to write down; its numeric value is not its encoded length.
3. **Worst case, asymptotically.** We count the steps an algorithm takes on its *worst* input of a given size, and only care how that count grows as the size grows.

A thousand needs only ten bits in binary. Doubling a positive integer adds one bit to its encoding: a small increase in written input can represent a much larger numeric value.

**Big O** describes an eventual upper bound on growth, allowing a fixed multiplying constant. The formal definition below is useful reference; it does not predict a stopwatch time.

```formula reference
T(n) = O(f(n))   means
T(n) ≤ cf(n)   for all n ≥ n_0
where
T(n): the worst-case number of steps the algorithm takes on any input of n bits
n: the input size, in bits
f(n): the growth benchmark function, such as n^2 or 2^n
O(f(n)): Big O of f(n): "grows at most as fast as a constant times f(n), once n is large enough"
c: a fixed positive constant that does not depend on n
n_0: a threshold size; the bound only has to hold for inputs at least this big
≤: is less than or equal to
≥: is greater than or equal to
In words: beyond some input size, the running time never exceeds a fixed constant times the chosen growth benchmark. This is an eventual upper bound, not an exact count or a claim that the bound is tight.
```

Big O ignores constant factors and small inputs on purpose: it describes the shape of the growth, not the exact time on a particular machine.

For problems such as integer-weight TSP with a known finite cost range, a threshold decision procedure lets you recover the optimum cost by binary search. The answers are monotone: once a budget is sufficient, every larger budget is sufficient. Each query can therefore discard half the remaining range. This uses a polynomial number of calls when the cost bound has polynomial bit length. Finding an actual solution additionally needs a suitable self-reduction; the statement is not a universal equivalence for arbitrary optimisation problems.

## Key takeaways

- Measure input size in bits, so large values can have short encodings.
- Big O bounds eventual worst-case growth, ignoring fixed factors.
- Binary search can recover an integer optimum cost from a threshold decision procedure.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

questions.prompt: A tour-cost decision procedure says whether some tour fits a proposed budget. Costs are nonnegative integers with a known upper bound, and at least one tour exists. Why can binary search find the optimum cost?

options.text: The procedure returns an optimal tour with each answer
options.explanation: It returns only yes or no, so recovering a tour requires additional work.

options.text: Once a budget works, every larger budget works too
options.explanation: This monotonicity lets each middle-budget query eliminate half the remaining cost range.

options.text: Every possible budget must be tested
options.explanation: Monotonicity allows entire intervals to be ruled out at once.

options.text: Every optimisation problem has the same reduction
options.explanation: The argument uses integer costs, a known bounded range and an appropriate threshold decision procedure.

Querying the middle repeatedly narrows the interval to the first yes-answer, the optimum cost. This uses logarithmically many calls in the known integer cost range; it does not itself return a tour.

lessons.title: What polynomial time promises
lessons.summary: P contains decision problems with deterministic polynomial-time algorithms.
lessons.body:
## P: the problems we can solve efficiently

**P** (polynomial time) is the set of decision problems solvable by a deterministic algorithm (one with no randomness or guessing) whose worst-case running time is bounded by a polynomial in the input size.

```formula essential
T(n) = O(n^k)   for some k
where
T(n): the worst-case number of steps the algorithm takes on an input of n bits
n: the input size, in bits
k: a constant exponent that does not grow with n, such as 1, 2 or 3
n^k: k copies of n multiplied together (n to the power k)
O(...): Big O: "at most a constant times this, for large n"
In words: a problem is in P when some deterministic algorithm solves every input in at most about n to the power k steps, for one fixed k. Sorting-style O(n^2) and shortest-path-style O(n^3) bounds qualify; 2 to the power n does not.
```

Why draw the line at polynomials?

- **Closure.** A polynomial-time algorithm that calls a polynomial-time subroutine a polynomial number of times is still polynomial. Compose efficient pieces and you stay efficient.
- **Robustness.** Standard classical models, such as Turing machines and bounded-word random-access models with explicit operation costs, simulate each other with polynomial overhead. The broader claim that classical computation efficiently simulates every physically realisable computation is an extended Church–Turing thesis, not a theorem; quantum computation challenges it.
- **Growth matters.** A cubic cost multiplies by a fixed factor when input length doubles. A cost exponential in input length eventually outgrows every fixed polynomial. Faster hardware changes constants, not this distinction.

Problems known to be in P include shortest paths, maximum matching, 2-SAT, linear programming (proven in 1979 with the ellipsoid method) and primality testing (the AKS algorithm, 2002).

> [!warning] Polynomial is not the same as fast
> A polynomial with exponent one hundred is in P but useless. In practice, natural problems in P tend to have small exponents, which is part of why the definition has stuck. Treat membership in P as a growth classification; check the exponent, constants and actual workload before deciding that an algorithm is practical.

## Key takeaways

- P contains decision problems with deterministic polynomial-time algorithms.
- Polynomial time is robust under composition but need not be practical.
- Primality is in P even though trial division is exponential in the bit length.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

questions.prompt: One exact algorithm has cubic growth in input length; another doubles its work for each extra input bit. What should you predict as inputs keep growing?

options.text: Their costs remain within a fixed factor
options.explanation: An exponential growth law eventually outgrows every fixed polynomial.

options.text: The exponential algorithm eventually grows faster than the cubic one
options.explanation: Hardware speed changes constants, while this distinction concerns growth with input length.

options.text: The cubic algorithm must always be practical
options.explanation: A polynomial bound can still have large constants or exceed the available resources.

options.text: Buying a faster processor makes both growth rates polynomial
options.explanation: A fixed speed multiplier does not change how work scales with input size.

questions.workedExample: Doubling the input length multiplies a cubic cost by eight. For a cost that doubles with each added input bit, doubling the input length causes an increasingly large multiplier. Faster hardware can postpone the difficulty, but cannot change either growth law.

questions.prompt: Trial division tests whether a whole number N is prime by trying every divisor up to the square root of N, about that many divisions. Is this a polynomial-time primality test, and is primality in P?

options.text: Yes and yes: the square root of the numeric value is a polynomial
options.explanation: The square root of N is polynomial in the *value* N, but writing N takes only about as many bits as its base-2 logarithm. Measured in bits b, the square root is about 2 to the power b/2: exponential in the input size.

options.text: No, and primality is not known to be in P
options.explanation: Trial division isn't polynomial, but primality *is* in P: the AKS algorithm (2002) proved it.

options.text: No, it's exponential in the number of bits; but primality is in P, by the AKS algorithm (2002)
options.explanation: The number of divisors tried grows exponentially with bit length in the worst case. AKS is a different algorithm proving that the primality decision problem belongs to P.

options.text: Yes, because each division is O(1)
options.explanation: Even if each division took size-independent operation time, there are about the square root of N of them, which is exponential in the bit-length.

questions.workedExample: Trial division works up to the square root of the number’s value. Binary encoding grows much more slowly than that value: adding two bits can roughly double the number of candidate divisors. So this algorithm is not polynomial in bit length. That says nothing decisive about the best algorithm: AKS supplies a different polynomial-time primality test.

lessons.title: Values versus bit lengths
lessons.summary: Subset sum’s table depends on the target value, not just its bit length.
lessons.body:
### The unary trap: pseudo-polynomial time

**Subset sum** asks: given a list of nonnegative integers and a nonnegative target total, does some selection add up to exactly the target? A textbook dynamic program fills a table with one row per number and one column per possible total, so its running time grows with the *value* of the target. That looks polynomial, but a positive target’s bit length grows only logarithmically:

```formula reference
t = O(nT)
T < 2^b
where
t: the running time of the dynamic program, in steps
n: how many numbers are in the input list
T: the target total (a value, not a length)
b: the number of bits used to write T in the input
2^b: 2 to the power b; a b-bit number is always smaller than this
O(...): Big O: "at most a constant times this, for large inputs"
In words: table work grows with the item count times the target value. The target value can be exponential in its encoded bit length, so this is not a polynomial-time bound for general binary inputs. Bit-operation analysis also accounts for counter and integer lengths.
```

Adding one bit to the target can roughly double the table width. A target fixed below a small bound is a useful special case, but does not establish polynomial time when its bit length grows.

Such algorithms are **pseudo-polynomial**: polynomial in the *value* of the numbers, not their length. Subset sum is not known to be in P.

## Key takeaways

- Subset sum’s table depends on the target value, not just its bit length.
- Pseudo-polynomial time can be exponential for binary inputs.
- A fixed numeric bound and a growing bit-width describe different input families.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

questions.prompt: For nonnegative Subset Sum, a dynamic program builds one row per item and one column per total up to the target. The target is written in binary and its bit width can grow. Does the table size establish polynomial time in the encoded input length?

options.text: Yes: multiplying two quantities mentioned in the input always gives a polynomial bound
options.explanation: The target is a value, not an encoded length. Binary notation can describe a huge value with relatively few bits.

options.text: No: adding one target bit can roughly double the number of table columns
options.explanation: Correct. The target value can grow exponentially in its binary length. This table bound is pseudo-polynomial; Subset Sum is not known to be in P.

options.text: Yes, because every practical target has some fixed finite bit width
options.explanation: A separately restricted family with a fixed target bound has bounded table width. That does not establish polynomial time when target bit width can grow.

options.text: No, because dynamic programming is never polynomial
options.explanation: Many dynamic programs are polynomial. The issue here is that the table width depends on the target value rather than its encoded length.

questions.workedExample: The table has a column for each total up to the target, whereas the input writes that target compactly in binary. Adding a target bit can roughly double the table width. The dynamic program is useful for small targets, but its bound is pseudo-polynomial when target bit length can grow.

lessons.title: Checking certificates in NP
lessons.summary: NP requires polynomial-size certificates and a polynomial-time verifier.
lessons.body:
## NP: the problems whose answers we can check

A problem is in **NP** if every yes-instance has a short **certificate** (a witness) that a fast algorithm can check.

Formally, a problem L is in NP if there is a polynomial-time **verifier** V (a checking algorithm) and a polynomial p such that:

```formula essential
x ∈ L   iff   ∃ c with
  |c| ≤ p(|x|)   and   V(x, c) = 1
where
L: the problem, viewed as the set of inputs whose answer is yes (its language)
x: an input (a problem instance), written as a string of bits
∈: "is a member of"; x ∈ L means x is a yes-instance
∃: "there exists": at least one such c can be found
c: a certificate (witness): extra information offered as evidence that x is a yes-instance
|c|, |x|: the length of c or x, in bits
p: a fixed polynomial, such as p(m) = m^2, that caps how long a certificate may be
V(x, c): the verifier, a polynomial-time algorithm that reads x and c and outputs 1 (accept) or 0 (reject)
≤: is less than or equal to
In words: x is a yes-instance exactly when some certificate, of length bounded by a fixed polynomial in the length of x, makes the fast checker V say yes. For a no-instance, every certificate is rejected.
```

For subset sum, the certificate is the subset itself. Checking it is one addition per chosen element; additions on binary integers cost polynomially many bit operations:

```python
def verify_subset_sum(S, T, idx):
    # idx is decoded as a set of positions.
    # Reject indices outside the input list.
    n = len(S)
    if not all(0 <= i < n for i in idx):
        return False
    return sum(S[i] for i in idx) == T

S, T = [3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2], 9
print(verify_subset_sum(S, T, {2, 4}))
# True: 4 + 5 = 9
print(verify_subset_sum(S, T, {0, 1}))
# False: 3 + 34 = 37
```

The verifier never searches. It only checks. Finding a good certificate by brute force means trying subsets: each extra input item doubles the number of choices. Checking one proposed subset still needs only polynomial work.

> [!note] NP does not stand for "not polynomial"
> NP means **nondeterministic polynomial time**. The equivalent original definition: a nondeterministic Turing machine (one that can "guess" at each step) accepts in polynomial time. Guess the certificate, then run the verifier. Every problem in P is also in NP, so "NP" is not a label for hard problems.

Other NP problems and their certificates:

| Problem | Certificate |
|---|---|
| SAT | A satisfying assignment |
| Hamiltonian cycle | The cycle's vertex order |
| 3-colouring | A colour per vertex |
| Composite number | A factor other than 1 and itself |

For the last row, check that the supplied factor is strictly between one and the input number and divides it exactly. For example, seven is a certificate that 91 is composite.

To check a Hamiltonian-cycle certificate, confirm its list contains every graph vertex exactly once, then check each consecutive edge and the last-to-first edge. With expected constant-time hash look-ups this takes expected linear work in the vertex count. A deterministic polynomial-time implementation also suffices for NP membership; finding the cycle is a different task.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A completed jigsaw
> Checking a proposed arrangement is different from finding one among all possible arrangements.
>
> **How it maps:** The completed arrangement acts as a certificate. A checker inspects whether it obeys the rules without having to search for that arrangement.
>
> **Where it stops:** The analogy does not prove any puzzle is hard. NP requires a precise polynomial bound on certificate length and checking time, and includes easy problems too.

The Python demonstration expects its certificate argument to have been decoded as a set of distinct integer positions, with an encoded size bounded polynomially in the input. A full verifier first rejects malformed encodings; a list containing repeated positions is not that certificate format. The examples use sets, so an input element cannot be counted twice.

## Key takeaways

- NP requires polynomial-size certificates and a polynomial-time verifier.
- A verifier checks a supplied candidate; it need not find one.
- Every P problem is in NP because the verifier can solve it directly.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

questions.prompt: A colleague says: "The decision problem of testing whether a list is sorted is in P, so it can't be in NP, because NP is the class of problems that aren't polynomial." What is wrong with this?

options.text: Nothing; P and NP are disjoint by definition
options.explanation: P and NP are not disjoint. Treating them as opposites is exactly the misreading of 'NP' as 'non-polynomial'.

options.text: NP means nondeterministic polynomial time, and every problem in P is also in NP
options.explanation: Correct. A verifier can ignore the certificate and solve the problem directly, so it is a proven fact that every problem in P is also in NP.

options.text: No decision problem about sorting can be discussed using P or NP
options.explanation: The prompt explicitly asks a decision problem. It is in P and therefore also NP.

options.text: It is only wrong if P equals NP
options.explanation: Every problem in P is in NP unconditionally. Whether NP contains problems outside P (whether the containment is strict) is the open question, not whether the containment holds.

questions.workedExample: A polynomial-time solver can serve as a verifier: ignore the certificate and solve the input directly. Yes-instances are accepted and no-instances rejected, so every P problem meets the NP definition. Whether NP contains additional problems is the open question.

questions.prompt: You are given a graph with n vertices and a claimed Hamiltonian cycle listing its vertices in order. Assume expected constant-time hash-set look-ups. What expected work checks this one claim?

options.text: O(n!), because there are n! orderings to try
options.explanation: That is the cost of *searching* for a cycle by brute force. Checking one given cycle does not search.

options.text: O(2ⁿ), because the problem is NP-complete
options.explanation: NP-completeness says solving is believed hard; it says nothing about checking, which is fast for every NP problem by definition.

options.text: O(n): check valid distinct vertices and every cycle edge
options.explanation: For n graph vertices, check the list length, vertex membership and distinctness, then each consecutive edge including last to first. Under the stated hash assumption this is expected linear work; polynomial deterministic verification is also possible.

options.text: It cannot be checked faster than it can be found
options.explanation: The whole point of NP is that checking can be (and for Hamiltonian cycle is) much easier than finding, as far as anyone knows.

questions.workedExample: Check the proposed list’s length, that every listed vertex is valid and appears once, and that every consecutive pair—including the last-to-first pair—is an edge. No search over other orders is needed. With expected constant-time hash look-ups, the check takes expected linear work in the vertex count; a deterministic polynomial-time check is also straightforward.

lessons.title: Certificates for no-answers
lessons.summary: coNP is the complement class of NP, with short certificates for no-instances.
lessons.body:
## coNP: short proofs of "no"

**coNP** contains the complements of NP problems: decision problems where every *no*-instance has a polynomial-size certificate that a deterministic polynomial-time verifier can check. UNSAT ("this formula has no satisfying assignment") and TAUTOLOGY are the standard examples.

The asymmetry is real. To convince you a formula is satisfiable, I hand you an assignment. To convince you it is *unsatisfiable*, nobody knows a short certificate in general; SAT solvers emit resolution proofs, but for some formulas (like the pigeonhole principle) every resolution proof is exponentially long.

Some problems are in both NP and coNP: both yes-answers and no-answers have short, quickly checkable certificates.

"Does N have a prime factor below k?" is one. For positive integers at least two, a yes-certificate is such a prime factor; a no-certificate is the full prime factorisation (each prime can itself be checked in polynomial time, by AKS). Problems in both NP and coNP are widely believed not to be NP-complete, since that would force NP and coNP to be equal.

## Key takeaways

- coNP is the complement class of NP, with short certificates for no-instances.
- General unsatisfiability is not known to have polynomial-size checkable certificates.
- Bounded-factor decision has certificates for both answers through prime factorisation.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

questions.prompt: A SAT solver reports that a 10,000-variable formula is **unsatisfiable**. Your auditor wants a certificate she can check in polynomial time. What does complexity theory say about this?

options.text: Easy: the solver can output the satisfying assignment it failed to find
options.explanation: There is no satisfying assignment to output; that is what unsatisfiable means. The yes-certificate for SAT doesn't help with 'no'.

options.text: UNSAT is in coNP; a polynomial-size certificate for every unsatisfiable formula exists only if NP equals coNP, which is conjectured false
options.explanation: Correct. Short 'no' certificates for all instances would put UNSAT in NP, and since UNSAT is coNP-complete that would make NP and coNP equal. In practice SAT solvers emit resolution-style proofs (DRAT), which are often fine but can be exponentially long in the worst case.

options.text: UNSAT is in P, so no certificate is needed
options.explanation: UNSAT is not known to be in P; if it were, flipping its answer would put SAT in P, and P would equal NP.

options.text: It's impossible to certify unsatisfiability at all
options.explanation: Certificates exist (for example a resolution refutation, or the full truth table); the question is whether they are polynomial-size in general.

questions.workedExample: A satisfying assignment is a certificate for SAT, hence for a no-answer to UNSAT. A polynomial-size, polynomial-time-checkable certificate for every unsatisfiable formula would also put UNSAT in NP. Because UNSAT is coNP-complete, this would force NP and coNP to coincide. Existing proof logs are checked in time polynomial in input plus proof size; their size need not be polynomial in the original formula.

questions.prompt: Consider the decision problem FACTOR: "given N and k, does N have a prime factor less than k?". Which statements are correct as of today? Select all that apply.

options.text: FACTOR is in NP
options.explanation: Correct. Certificate: a prime factor p < k; check p divides N and that p is prime (in P by AKS).

options.text: FACTOR is in coNP
options.explanation: Correct. Certificate for 'no': the full prime factorisation of N; check the product, check each factor is prime, and check none is below k.

options.text: FACTOR is proven not to be in P
options.explanation: No such lower bound is known. It's just that no polynomial-time classical algorithm has been found; the best known (the general number field sieve) has a heuristic expected subexponential bound.

options.text: If FACTOR were NP-complete, then NP equals coNP
options.explanation: Correct. Every NP problem would reduce to FACTOR, which is in coNP, putting all of NP inside coNP, and hence making the two classes equal. This is why FACTOR is believed not to be NP-complete.

options.text: RSA's security is proven to follow from P differs from NP
options.explanation: Wrong. Easy factoring breaks RSA, but factoring hardness alone is not known to imply RSA inversion hardness. P differs from NP guarantees neither the required average-case hardness nor security of the scheme.

questions.workedExample: For yes, supply a prime factor below the threshold and check primality and divisibility. For no, supply the full prime factorisation, check its product and each prime, and confirm none is below the threshold. The factor list has polynomial encoded length. Thus both answer types have certificates. NP-completeness would then collapse NP and coNP; classical polynomial-time factoring and RSA inversion hardness remain separate unresolved questions.

lessons.title: Proven containments and open separations
lessons.summary: P is contained in NP, PSPACE and EXPTIME; P differs from EXPTIME.
lessons.body:
## What is proven, and what isn't

The proven facts fit in one chain of classes, plus one separation:

```formula essential
P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME
P ≠ EXPTIME
P = NP   gives   NP = coNP
where
P: the complexity class P: decision problems a deterministic algorithm solves in polynomial time (at most about n^k steps for some fixed k)
NP: the class NP: decision problems whose yes-answers have a short certificate checkable in polynomial time
coNP: the class coNP: decision problems whose no-answers have a short certificate checkable in polynomial time
PSPACE: decision problems solvable using a polynomial amount of memory (at most about n^k bits), however long it takes
EXPTIME: decision problems solvable in exponential time: at most about 2 to the power n^k steps for some fixed k
⊆: "is contained in": every problem in the left class is also in the right class (the two may turn out to be equal)
≠: "is not equal to": here, some problem is in EXPTIME but not in P
n: the input size, in bits
k: a fixed constant exponent
In words: each class in the chain sits inside the next; P is definitely smaller than EXPTIME; and if P were equal to NP, then NP would also equal coNP.
```

Why each piece holds:

- **P is inside NP.** If you can solve the problem, the verifier can ignore the certificate and solve it.
- **NP is inside EXPTIME.** Try every possible polynomial-length certificate.
- **P is not all of EXPTIME.** The *time hierarchy theorem* (Hartmanis and Stearns, 1965) shows that more time solves strictly more problems.
- So in the chain, **at least one** inclusion is strict. Nobody knows which.
- **If P equals NP, NP equals coNP**, because P is closed under complement: flip the answer of a polynomial-time algorithm and it is still polynomial-time.

Enumerating polynomial-length certificates takes exponentially many trials. Running a polynomial-time checker on each still gives an exponential-time algorithm. The distinction is between the time for one check and the number of candidates.

Open problems:

- **P vs NP.** Almost all experts conjecture P differs from NP. It is one of the Clay Millennium Prize problems ($1 million).
- **NP vs coNP.** Conjectured different.
- Whether graph isomorphism or factoring is in P. Neither is known to be NP-complete; Babai (2015, with a fix in 2017) put graph isomorphism in quasi-polynomial time (below).

**Quasi-polynomial time** is a useful upper-bound category between polynomial and ordinary exponential scales. It includes polynomial bounds; proving such an upper bound never proves a problem needs that much time.

```formula reference
t = 2^{O((log n)^c)}
where
t: the running time, in steps
n: the input size, in bits
log: the logarithm (base 2 here; the base only changes the constant)
c: a fixed constant; for c = 1 this is just a polynomial
O(...): Big O: "at most a constant times this, for large n"
2^{...}: 2 raised to that power
In words: exponentiating a fixed power of the logarithm gives a quasi-polynomial bound. These bounds include polynomials and also growth faster than every polynomial but slower than ordinary exponential growth. An upper bound never proves that much time is necessary.
```

The practical lesson is to distinguish an algorithm’s upper bound from a lower bound on every possible algorithm.

```
+-------------- EXPTIME -------------+
| +------------ PSPACE ------------+ |
| | +---- NP -----+                | |
| | |        +----+---- coNP --+   | |
| | |        | P  |            |   | |
| | |        +----+------------+   | |
| | +-------------+                | |
| +--------------------------------+ |
+------------------------------------+
 P sits inside NP ∩ coNP. The picture
 assumes P != NP != coNP; of the
 separations, only P != EXPTIME is
 proven.
```

The NP-to-PSPACE inclusion reuses memory: enumerate every polynomial-size certificate in turn, run the polynomial-time checker, then reuse its workspace for the next. The number of trials affects time, while the storage for one certificate and one checker run stays polynomial.

## Key takeaways

- P is contained in NP, PSPACE and EXPTIME; P differs from EXPTIME.
- Neither P versus NP nor NP versus coNP has been resolved.
- An upper bound such as quasi-polynomial time does not establish a matching lower bound.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

questions.prompt: Which of these statements are **proven** theorems (not conjectures)? Select all that apply.

options.text: P is contained in NP
options.explanation: Proven: a verifier can ignore the certificate and solve the problem itself.

options.text: P differs from NP
options.explanation: Not proven. It is the most famous open problem in computer science, though almost all experts conjecture it.

options.text: NP is contained in EXPTIME
options.explanation: Proven: try every certificate of length up to p(n), the polynomial certificate-length limit. That is exponentially many runs of a polynomial-time verifier, which is still exponential time.

options.text: P differs from EXPTIME
options.explanation: Proven by the time hierarchy theorem: with exponentially more time you can solve strictly more problems.

options.text: NP differs from coNP
options.explanation: Not proven. It is conjectured, and it would imply P differs from NP, so proving it is at least as hard.

questions.workedExample: A solver can ignore a certificate, proving P is inside NP. Enumerating all polynomial-length certificates gives an exponential-time solver, proving NP is inside EXPTIME. The time hierarchy theorem proves P differs from EXPTIME. None of these arguments determines whether P equals NP or NP equals coNP.

questions.prompt: Suppose someone proves that P equals NP. Which of the following then **must** be true?

options.text: NP equals coNP
options.explanation: Correct. P is closed under complement (flip the answer of a deterministic algorithm), so coNP becomes the complement class of P, which is P itself, which equals NP.

options.text: Every NP problem can be solved in quadratic time
options.explanation: Membership in P promises some fixed polynomial exponent, not a quadratic bound or a small constant.

options.text: P equals EXPTIME
options.explanation: The time hierarchy theorem proves P differs from EXPTIME unconditionally; P equals NP can't change that.

options.text: We would immediately have a practical SAT algorithm
options.explanation: The proof might be non-constructive or give a huge exponent or constant. It would be revolutionary, but not necessarily practical.

questions.workedExample: Assume P equals NP. A coNP problem’s complement is then in P; swapping that deterministic solver’s answers puts the original problem in P too. Conversely every P problem is in coNP by the same complement argument. Therefore NP equals coNP. This promises neither a small exponent nor a practical algorithm, and cannot overturn the proven separation from EXPTIME.

lessons.title: Proof barriers and practical hardness
lessons.summary: Relativisation, natural proofs and algebrisation limit families of proof techniques.
lessons.body:
### Why it is so hard to prove

Three known **barriers** rule out whole families of proof techniques:

- **Relativisation** (Baker, Gill and Solovay, 1975): there are oracles (imaginary black-box subroutines) relative to which P equals NP, and others where they differ, so simulation-and-diagonalisation arguments like the halting proof cannot settle it.
- **Natural proofs** (Razborov and Rudich, 1994): a broad class of circuit lower-bound arguments would, if they worked, break pseudorandom functions that are believed secure.
- **Algebrisation** (Aaronson and Wigderson, 2008) extends the relativisation barrier.

## Why practitioners care

- **Recognising the wall.** If your scheduling problem is NP-complete (in the NP-completeness units), stop hunting for a fast exact algorithm for all inputs and reach for approximations, heuristics or solvers (in the coping-strategy units).
- **Cryptography.** Standard computationally secure encryption with short reusable keys requires one-way functions; information-theoretic schemes such as the one-time pad use different key-length assumptions. If one-way functions exist then P and NP are different. The converse is not known: P differs from NP alone would not guarantee secure cryptography, because NP-hardness is about the worst case and crypto needs problems hard on *average*.
- **Worst case is not typical case.** Modern SAT solvers handle many large industrial instances; performance depends strongly on structure and workload. If P and NP differ, NP-hardness rules out a polynomial-time exact algorithm for all inputs; it does not say this particular instance is hard.

## Key takeaways

- Relativisation, natural proofs and algebrisation limit families of proof techniques.
- Worst-case hardness does not establish cryptographic average-case hardness.
- NP-completeness guides algorithm choices without predicting every instance’s difficulty.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

questions.prompt: Baker, Gill and Solovay (1975) showed there is an oracle A relative to which P and NP are equal, and an oracle B relative to which they are different. What does this imply for attempts to resolve P vs NP?

options.text: P vs NP is independent of the axioms of mathematics
options.explanation: Oracle results say nothing about provability in ZFC. Whether P vs NP is formally independent is unknown.

options.text: Any proof technique that works equally well relative to every oracle (like pure simulation and diagonalisation) cannot settle P vs NP
options.explanation: Correct. Such a 'relativising' proof that P and NP differ would also prove they differ relative to oracle A, which is false; similarly a relativising proof that they are equal fails relative to oracle B.

options.text: P equals NP, because we found an oracle where they're equal
options.explanation: An oracle world is a different model of computation. It doesn't settle the unrelativised question either way.

options.text: Diagonalisation cannot prove any separation of complexity classes
options.explanation: Diagonalisation does prove P differs from EXPTIME (time hierarchy). It just can't separate P from NP on its own.

questions.workedExample: A relativising argument would apply unchanged when both machine types receive the same oracle. One oracle makes the classes equal and another separates them. Either proposed conclusion would therefore be false in one of those worlds. This blocks that family of arguments, not all proofs or provability in ordinary mathematics.

questions.prompt: A startup claims: "Our encryption is unbreakable because breaking it is NP-hard, and P differs from NP." Setting aside that P differs from NP is unproven, what is the deeper flaw?

options.text: NP-hard problems can always be solved by SAT solvers
options.explanation: SAT solvers handle many instances but have no general guarantee. This doesn't capture the real flaw in the argument.

options.text: NP-hardness is a worst-case notion; cryptography needs problems that are hard on almost all randomly generated keys
options.explanation: Correct. P differs from NP only guarantees *some* hard instances exist. A cipher whose typical keys give easy instances is insecure. Crypto needs average-case hardness, formalised as one-way functions, which is a stronger assumption than P differs from NP.

options.text: Encryption has nothing to do with complexity theory
options.explanation: Modern cryptography is built on complexity assumptions. If P equalled NP, most public-key and symmetric schemes would be breakable in principle.

options.text: Quantum computers solve all NP-hard problems
options.explanation: There's no evidence that quantum computers solve NP-hard problems efficiently; BQP is not believed to contain NP.

questions.workedExample: Worst-case hardness means an efficient algorithm cannot solve every instance under the stated assumption. An attacker faces instances produced by the scheme’s key generator. If that distribution frequently produces easy instances, hard instances elsewhere offer no protection. One-way functions require appropriate average-case hardness; their existence implies P differs from NP, but the converse is unknown.

lessons.title: Reading and composing reductions
lessons.summary: A many-one reduction preserves yes and no answers through one polynomial-time translation.
lessons.body:
Thousands of problems in NP have resisted polynomial-time algorithms: scheduling, routing, packing, colouring, satisfiability. Cook’s 1971 theorem began a way to relate such problems: an efficient algorithm for any NP-complete problem would give one for every problem in NP.

The tool that ties them together is the **polynomial-time reduction**, and the problems at the top of the pile are called **NP-complete**.

## Reductions: "B is at least as hard as A"

A **polynomial-time (many-one, or Karp) reduction** from problem A to problem B is a function f such that:

- f is computable in polynomial time, and
- for every input x: x is a yes-instance of A **if and only if** f(x) is a yes-instance of B.

In symbols:

```formula essential
A ≤_p B
x ∈ A  iff  f(x) ∈ B   for every x
where
A, B: decision problems, each viewed as the set of inputs whose answer is yes
≤_p: "polynomial-time reduces to": A ≤_p B means a polynomial-time translation maps every instance of A to an instance of B with the same yes/no answer, so B is at least as hard as A
x: any input (instance) of problem A, written as a string of bits
f: the reduction: a function, computable in polynomial time, that turns an instance of A into an instance of B
f(x): the instance of B that f produces from x
∈: "is a member of": x ∈ A means x is a yes-instance of A
In words: A reduces to B when a fast translation f turns every question about A into a question about B with exactly the same answer.
```

Read the reduction notation as "A is no harder than B", because any algorithm for B gives one for A: compute f(x), then ask B.

For example, Hamiltonian cycle (is there a cycle visiting every vertex exactly once?) reduces to TSP (is there a tour of tour cost at most some budget?). Given a graph with 10 vertices, f gives every edge weight 1, every missing edge weight 2, and sets the budget to 10. A tour of cost 10 must use only weight-1 edges, so the TSP answer is yes exactly when the graph has a Hamiltonian cycle.

```
 x --[ f: poly time ]--> f(x)
 f(x) --[ solver for B ]--> yes/no
 together: an algorithm for A
```

Two properties do most of the work:

- **Transitive**: if A reduces to B and B reduces to C, then A reduces to C. Compose the two translations; a polynomial of a polynomial is a polynomial.
- **Downward closure of P**: if A reduces to B and B can be solved in polynomial time, so can A.

Why composition stays polynomial: the first translation cannot write more output than it has time to write. The second therefore receives only polynomially many bits; a polynomial in that length is still a polynomial in the original length.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Translating an application form
> An office accepts only its own form. A translator copies your request into that format without changing what is being requested, then the office decides it.
>
> **How it maps:** The translation is the reduction, the office is the target solver, and its decision answers the original question. A better office procedure would therefore help everyone whose forms can be translated.
>
> **Where it stops:** A mathematical reduction must preserve both yes and no answers for every input and run in polynomial time. Ordinary paperwork does not guarantee either property.

## Key takeaways

- A many-one reduction preserves yes and no answers through one polynomial-time translation.
- An algorithm for the target solves the source problem.
- Polynomial output length makes composition stay polynomial.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Theory of Computation — MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/)

questions.prompt: You find a polynomial-time reduction f from problem A to problem B, and you know B is in P. What can you conclude?

options.text: B is NP-hard
options.explanation: Reducing A to B says B is at least as hard as A. Without knowing A is NP-hard, nothing about B's hardness follows.

options.text: Nothing, unless A is also in P
options.explanation: The reduction gives A's membership in P directly; there's nothing extra to assume.

options.text: A is in P
options.explanation: Correct. To decide whether an input x is a yes-instance of A, compute f(x) in polynomial time, then run B's polynomial algorithm on f(x). The composition is polynomial.

options.text: A and B are equally hard
options.explanation: A reduction from A to B only bounds A's difficulty from above by B's. B might be much harder than A.

questions.workedExample: First translate the source input. The translation takes polynomial time, so its output cannot be more than polynomially long. Run the target’s polynomial-time solver on that output and return its answer. Answer preservation gives correctness; composing the two polynomial bounds gives a polynomial-time source algorithm.

questions.prompt: You suspect your new problem ROSTER is NP-hard. Which reduction should you build?

options.text: From ROSTER to 3-SAT
options.explanation: This shows ROSTER is no harder than 3-SAT, which is true of every problem in NP. It's the classic wrong-direction mistake.

options.text: From 3-SAT (or another known NP-complete problem) to ROSTER
options.explanation: Correct. Turning any 3-SAT instance into an equivalent ROSTER instance shows a fast ROSTER algorithm would solve 3-SAT, so ROSTER is at least as hard.

options.text: From ROSTER to ROSTER
options.explanation: The identity map is a reduction from any problem to itself and proves nothing.

options.text: Either direction works, because reductions are symmetric
options.explanation: Reductions are not symmetric. Everything in P reduces to SAT, but SAT is not believed to reduce to problems in P.

questions.workedExample: Imagine a fast ROSTER solver. To use it for 3-SAT, you must turn each formula into a roster instance without solving the formula first. Prove that satisfiable formulas give feasible rosters and that a feasible output roster implies the original formula was satisfiable. This establishes hardness; a separate certificate argument establishes NP membership.

lessons.title: NP-hardness versus NP-completeness
lessons.summary: NP-complete means both NP-hard and in NP.
lessons.body:
## NP-hard and NP-complete

- A problem B is **NP-hard** if *every* problem in NP reduces to it.
- B is **NP-complete** if it is NP-hard **and** in NP.

These are separate obligations: hardness transfers the difficulty of other problems; membership supplies a polynomial-size certificate and polynomial-time checker.

The consequence: if any single NP-complete problem is in P, then every NP problem is in P, so P and NP are the same class. Conversely, if they differ, no NP-complete problem has a polynomial-time algorithm.

> [!warning] NP-hard does not mean "in NP and hard"
> The halting problem is NP-hard (any NP problem reduces to it: build a machine that halts iff the instance is a yes) but is not in NP; it isn't even decidable. An optimisation problem such as finding a shortest tour is NP-hard because solving it would solve an NP-hard decision problem. Merely being an optimisation problem does not make it hard. NP membership itself is defined for decision problems.

## Key takeaways

- NP-complete means both NP-hard and in NP.
- An undecidable problem may be NP-hard, and optimisation uses a different problem type.
- One NP-complete decision problem in P would imply P equals NP.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Theory of Computation — MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/)

questions.prompt: You have reduced 3-SAT to a new decision problem in polynomial time, preserving both answers. What is still needed before calling the new problem NP-complete?

options.text: Prove it has no polynomial-time algorithm
options.explanation: That would resolve P versus NP, and is not part of an NP-completeness proof.

options.text: Show polynomial-size yes-certificates have a polynomial-time verifier
options.explanation: The reduction establishes NP-hardness; this separate argument establishes membership in NP.

options.text: Test that the solver is slow on several examples
options.explanation: Measurements on selected inputs do not establish the class membership required for NP-completeness.

options.text: Show every instance is difficult
options.explanation: Worst-case completeness does not require every input to be hard.

questions.workedExample: The reduction transfers hardness: an algorithm for the new problem could solve the known NP-complete source. But hardness alone does not provide a short certificate or a verifier for the new problem. Establish those separately to conclude NP-completeness.

questions.prompt: Which of these problems are known to be **NP-hard**? Select all that apply.

options.text: SAT
options.explanation: NP-hard (in fact NP-complete) by the Cook–Levin theorem.

options.text: The halting problem
options.explanation: NP-hard: any NP problem reduces to it by mapping x to a machine that halts iff x is a yes-instance. It is not in NP (it's undecidable), so it is NP-hard but not NP-complete.

options.text: 2-SAT
options.explanation: 2-SAT is in P (linear time via strongly connected components). It would be NP-hard only if P equals NP, which nobody believes.

options.text: Finding a minimum-length travelling-salesman tour
options.explanation: NP-hard: it's an optimisation problem whose decision version is NP-complete. It isn't in NP itself because it isn't a yes/no problem.

options.text: Shortest path between two vertices with nonnegative weights
options.explanation: In P (Dijkstra). Like 2-SAT, it's not NP-hard unless P equals NP.

questions.workedExample: SAT is NP-complete. For Halting, write a machine that decides the given NP instance, halts on yes and loops on no: writing that description is fast even if running it is slow. Optimising a TSP tour also solves its hard threshold decision version. In contrast, 2-SAT and nonnegative shortest-path decision are in P, so hardness for either would imply P equals NP.

lessons.title: Encoding a computation as SAT
lessons.summary: Cook–Levin proves SAT NP-complete by encoding accepting computations.
lessons.body:
## The Cook–Levin theorem

**Theorem (Cook 1971; Levin independently, published 1973).** SAT, deciding whether a Boolean formula has a satisfying assignment, is NP-complete.

SAT is in NP: the assignment is the certificate. The hard part is showing every NP problem reduces to SAT. We can't know each problem in advance, so the proof works from the only thing they share: a nondeterministic Turing machine N that decides L within a polynomial number of steps.

### The tableau

An accepting run of N on an input w is a sequence of configurations (snapshots of the state, head position and tape), one per step. Write them as the rows of a square grid, the **tableau**. Each cell holds one symbol: a tape symbol, or a state marker showing where the head is. With a time bound at least the input length, both the number of rows and the number of tape positions are at most proportional to that bound. Initial and boundary cells add only constant-factor overhead.

```
       cell 1  2  3  4  5 ...
row 1   # q0 w1 w2 w3  _ ... #  start
row 2   #  a q3 w2 w3  _ ... #
row 3   #  a  b q7 w3  _ ... #
 ...
row t   #  .  . qacc   ...   #  accept
```

The formula has one Boolean variable per (cell, symbol) pair, and is the AND of four parts:

```formula essential
x_{i,j,s} = 1  iff  T_{i,j} = s
φ = φ_cell ∧ φ_start ∧ φ_accept ∧ φ_move
where
x_{i,j,s}: a Boolean variable, one for each cell and each possible symbol; 1 means true, 0 means false
T_{i,j}: the symbol written in the tableau cell at row i, column j
i: the row number, naming a configuration in the run
j: the column number, naming a tape position
s: one symbol from the fixed set of possible cell symbols (tape symbols and state markers)
φ: phi, the whole Boolean formula the reduction outputs
φ_cell, φ_start, φ_accept, φ_move: the four parts of φ, described in the list below
∧: AND: φ is true only when all four parts are true
In words: x_{i,j,s} says "cell (i, j) holds symbol s", and φ is true exactly when the variables describe a legal accepting run.
```

- **φ_cell**: every cell holds exactly one symbol.
- **φ_start**: row 1 is the start configuration on w.
- **φ_accept**: the accept state appears somewhere.
- **φ_move**: every 2 × 3 **window** of adjacent cells is consistent with N's transition function. Because a Turing machine changes only the cells around its head in one step, checking all these small local windows is enough to guarantee that each row legally follows from the one before.

Here is how φ_cell is built for one cell, as CNF clauses over integer-named variables (positive means the variable, negative its negation):

```python
from itertools import combinations

def exactly_one(vs):
    # at least one symbol in the cell
    clauses = [list(vs)]
    # no two symbols at once
    for a, b in combinations(vs, 2):
        clauses.append([-a, -b])
    return clauses

print(exactly_one([1, 2, 3]))
# [[1, 2, 3], [-1, -2], [-1, -3], [-2, -3]]
```

## Key takeaways

- Cook–Levin proves SAT NP-complete by encoding accepting computations.
- Tableau cells encode symbols and machine state through Boolean variables.
- Exactly-one constraints and local transition windows describe legal runs.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Theory of Computation — MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/)

questions.prompt: A Cook–Levin encoding keeps every pairwise “not both symbols” clause but omits the “at least one symbol” clause for a cell. What invalid setting is now allowed?

options.text: Two symbols in that cell simultaneously
options.explanation: The retained pairwise clauses still forbid that.

options.text: A symbol from outside the machine alphabet
options.explanation: There are no variables for symbols outside the fixed alphabet in this construction.

options.text: No symbol in the cell at all
options.explanation: Setting all its symbol variables false satisfies every pairwise not-both clause.

options.text: An exponential alphabet
options.explanation: Omitting a clause does not change the machine’s fixed alphabet.

questions.workedExample: The remaining pairwise clauses say that no two symbols can both be selected. They do not require any symbol at all. Setting every cell-symbol variable false satisfies them, leaving a cell with no symbol. The missing at-least-one clause is needed to describe an actual configuration.

lessons.title: Why the tableau stays polynomial
lessons.summary: A polynomial-time run occupies a tableau of polynomial area.
lessons.body:
Continue the Cook–Levin encoding: each cell in a time-by-tape tableau has a fixed finite choice of symbols, represented by Boolean variables. The machine is fixed while its input grows. Exactly-one clauses and local transition checks enforce a legal accepting run.

### Why it's a polynomial reduction

The `exactly_one` encoding adds an at-least-one clause and forbids every pair of symbols from coexisting. The alphabet and machine rules are fixed, so this is a constant amount of work per cell as the input grows.

Add it up over the whole grid:

```formula essential
N_cells = O(n^{2k})
|φ| = O(C^2 n^{2k}) = O(n^{2k})
where
N_cells: the number of tableau cells, including start-row and boundary padding
n: the input length, in symbols
k: the fixed exponent of the machine's polynomial time bound
C: the number of possible cell symbols, a constant fixed by the machine
φ: phi, the Boolean formula the reduction builds
|φ|: the size of the formula φ: how many symbols it takes to write down
O(...): Big O: grows at most as fast as a constant times the expression inside, for large n
In words: each grid dimension is bounded by the polynomial runtime, so their product is still polynomial. A fixed amount of local formula per cell preserves that polynomial size bound.
```

Squaring a polynomial bound keeps it polynomial. This is a validity argument for the reduction, not a claim that materialising the tableau is an efficient practical SAT encoding.

A satisfying assignment *is* an accepting computation, read off cell by cell; and an accepting computation gives a satisfying assignment. Thus the input is accepted exactly when the constructed SAT instance is satisfiable.

> [!note] What the nondeterminism becomes
> N's guesses turn into the freedom the SAT solver has in choosing variable values. The formula is fixed; the "guessing" is the existential "is there an assignment?".

The formula-size counts use atomic Boolean variables and clauses. If every variable identifier is written explicitly in binary, identifier lengths can add a logarithmic factor to the bit length. The construction remains polynomial under either reasonable encoding.

## Key takeaways

- A polynomial-time run occupies a tableau of polynomial area.
- The machine’s alphabet and local rules are fixed constants.
- Satisfying assignments correspond to accepting runs in both directions.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Theory of Computation — MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/)

questions.prompt: Why is a Cook–Levin tableau still polynomial in input length when its machine runs in polynomial time?

options.text: It stores every possible computation in a separate row
options.explanation: Rows describe steps of one candidate run; all candidate runs are represented by different assignments.

options.text: Both grid dimensions are polynomial, with fixed local work per cell
options.explanation: Time bounds the rows and the reachable tape positions; the fixed machine gives constant local constraints.

options.text: SAT always has only polynomially many assignments
options.explanation: A polynomial-size formula may have exponentially many assignments.

options.text: The reduction first finds an accepting computation
options.explanation: The encoding is built without knowing which, if any, choices lead to acceptance.

questions.workedExample: The tableau has one dimension for time and one for tape positions. Each dimension is polynomially bounded, so their product is still polynomial. With a fixed machine, each cell adds only a constant number of local constraints. Exponentially many assignments to those variables do not make the written formula exponentially long.

questions.prompt: Why does the Cook–Levin proof need L to be decided in **polynomial** time by the nondeterministic machine, rather than, say, time 2ⁿ (where n is the input length)?

options.text: Because SAT can only express polynomial-time computations
options.explanation: A formula can describe a computation of any fixed length; the problem is the size of the formula, not expressiveness.

options.text: With time 2ⁿ the tableau, and hence the formula, would have about 4ⁿ cells, so building it would take exponential time and it would no longer be a polynomial-time reduction
options.explanation: Correct. A reduction must run in polynomial time, which bounds the formula's size. The tableau's side length is the running time, so a 2ⁿ-time machine gives a 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ grid.

options.text: Because nondeterministic machines can't run for exponential time
options.explanation: They can; NEXPTIME is exactly the class of problems decided by nondeterministic machines in exponential time.

options.text: It doesn't; the proof works for any time bound
options.explanation: The same encoding exists for any time bound, but only polynomial bounds give polynomial-size formulas, which is what makes it a Karp reduction.

questions.workedExample: Writing the whole tableau requires writing each time-by-tape cell and its local constraints. Squaring a polynomial bound stays polynomial; squaring an exponential bound stays exponential. The encoding still represents a computation, but would fail the polynomial-time requirement for a Karp reduction.

lessons.title: From SAT to 3-SAT and 2-SAT
lessons.summary: Fresh variables split long CNF clauses with only linear growth.
lessons.body:
## From SAT to 3-SAT

Most reductions start from **3-SAT**: CNF formulas where every clause has exactly 3 literals (in some treatments, at most 3). Its rigid shape makes gadgets easier to design.

First convert a general Boolean formula to equisatisfiable CNF with fresh gate variables (the Tseitin construction); distributing OR over AND can cause exponential blow-up. SAT in CNF then reduces to 3-SAT by splitting long clauses with fresh variables. A five-literal clause is replaced by three three-literal clauses:

```formula essential
C_old = (l_1 ∨ l_2 ∨ l_3 ∨ l_4 ∨ l_5)
C_new = (l_1 ∨ l_2 ∨ y_1)
  ∧ (¬y_1 ∨ l_3 ∨ y_2)
  ∧ (¬y_2 ∨ l_4 ∨ l_5)
where
C_old: the original clause, with 5 literals
C_new: the three clauses that replace it
l_1, l_2, l_3, l_4, l_5: the literals of the original clause; a literal is a variable or its negation
y_1, y_2: fresh variables that appear nowhere else in the formula
∨: OR: a clause is true when at least one of its literals is true
∧: AND: all three new clauses must be true
¬: NOT: ¬y_1 is true exactly when y_1 is false
In words: C_new can be satisfied (by choosing y_1 and y_2) exactly when at least one original literal is true, so C_old and C_new are equivalent for satisfiability.
```

If some l_i is true, set the y's to "carry" the chain round it: y's before it true, y's after it false. If all l_i are false, y_1 must be true, which forces y_2 true, which falsifies the last clause.

Each extra original literal needs only a constant amount of extra formula, so splitting has linear growth. Short clauses are padded by repeating a literal, or with extra variables if repeats are forbidden.

The fresh variables are local to this clause. Reusing them across unrelated clauses could introduce constraints that were never in the original formula. The new formula is equisatisfiable with the old one: assignments to original variables may need extending, rather than using the same assignment unchanged.

### The edge of tractability: 2-SAT

With two literals per clause, the problem collapses into P. Each two-literal clause is the same as two implications:

```formula essential
(a ∨ b)  ≡  (¬a → b) ∧ (¬b → a)
where
a, b: literals (a variable or its negation)
∨: OR: true when at least one side is true
¬: NOT: ¬a is true exactly when a is false
→: implies: ¬a → b means "if a is false then b must be true"
∧: AND: both implications hold
≡: "is logically equivalent to": true in exactly the same assignments
In words: "a or b" means "if not a then b, and if not b then a". For the clause (x ∨ y): if x is false, y must be true, and if y is false, x must be true.
```

Draw each implication as an arrow between literals: this is the implication graph. The formula is unsatisfiable exactly when some variable and its own negation lie in the same strongly connected component of this graph (each can reach the other), which takes linear time to check (Aspvall, Plass and Tarjan, 1979). Going from 2 to 3 literals per clause crosses from linear time to NP-complete.

## Key takeaways

- Fresh variables split long CNF clauses with only linear growth.
- The split preserves satisfiability through an extension of the original assignment.
- 2-SAT uses implication graphs and strongly connected components.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Theory of Computation — MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/)

questions.prompt: Why do fresh linking variables let a long CNF clause become a linear-size chain of three-literal clauses?

options.text: They force every original literal to be true
options.explanation: The original clause requires only one true literal.

options.text: They carry an unsatisfied clause forwards until some original literal satisfies it
options.explanation: The chain can be extended to a satisfying assignment exactly when at least one original literal is true.

options.text: They enumerate all assignments to the original variables
options.explanation: The construction is local and linear; it does not solve the formula.

options.text: They can be shared freely between unrelated clauses
options.explanation: Unrelated clauses need fresh variables to avoid introducing unwanted dependencies.

questions.workedExample: The first split clause passes an unsatisfied choice into a fresh variable; each middle clause passes it onwards. If all original literals are false, the final clause fails. If some original literal is true, the fresh variables can be set to satisfy the chain. Only constant work is added per original literal, so the translation remains linear in clause length.

Is this 2-SAT formula satisfiable?

```formula essential
F = (x ∨ y) ∧ (¬x ∨ y)
  ∧ (x ∨ ¬y) ∧ (¬x ∨ ¬y)
where
F: the whole formula
x, y: Boolean variables, each true or false
∨: OR: a clause is true when at least one side is true
∧: AND: all four clauses must be true
¬: NOT: ¬x is true exactly when x is false
In words: four two-literal clauses over x and y, all of which must hold.
```

Use the implication-graph method.

options.text: Yes, with x true and y true
options.explanation: This falsifies the last clause, (not x or not y).

If the first variable is false, the first clause forces the second variable true and the third forces it false. Thus either choice contradicts an implication. lessons.title: Proving a new problem complete
lessons.summary: Show NP membership and reduce a known NP-complete problem to the new problem.
lessons.body:
## Karp's 21 and the domino effect

In 1972 Richard Karp showed 21 well-known problems NP-complete by chaining reductions from SAT: clique, vertex cover, set cover, Hamiltonian cycle, graph colouring, knapsack, and more. Garey and Johnson's 1979 book catalogued hundreds. This lets each new proof reuse earlier work.

The recipe for showing a new problem X is NP-complete:

1. Show **X is in NP** (give the certificate and verifier).
2. Pick a known NP-complete problem Y.
3. Give a polynomial-time translation f **from Y to X**: transform instances of the *known* hard problem into instances of X.
4. Prove **both** directions: a yes-instance of Y maps to a yes-instance of X, and a yes-instance produced by f comes only from a yes-instance of Y.

The commonest mistake is reducing in the wrong direction. Reducing X to SAT only proves X is no harder than SAT, which is true of every problem in NP.

## Where you meet it in practice

- **Package managers.** Deciding whether a set of packages with versioned dependencies and conflicts can be installed together is NP-complete. libsolv (behind openSUSE's zypper and Fedora's dnf) solves it with a SAT solver.
- **Register allocation** is graph colouring in disguise (Chaitin, 1981); compilers use heuristics.
- **Puzzles**: generalised Sudoku and Minesweeper consistency are NP-complete.

## Key takeaways

- Show NP membership and reduce a known NP-complete problem to the new problem.
- Prove both directions and a polynomial construction bound.
- Dependency resolution, register allocation and generalised puzzles illustrate the method.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Theory of Computation — MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/)

questions.prompt: Your team's package manager hangs for minutes on some dependency sets. Resolving versioned dependencies with conflicts is NP-complete. A junior engineer proposes writing a "smarter" greedy resolver that is guaranteed polynomial time and always finds a valid install set when one exists. What's the right response?

options.text: Go ahead; greedy algorithms are optimal for dependency graphs
options.explanation: Dependency resolution with conflicts is NP-complete; greedy choices can paint you into a corner that needs backtracking.

options.text: That would prove P equals NP; instead encode the problem for a SAT solver (as libsolv does) and rely on its good typical-case performance, with time limits
options.explanation: Correct. A guaranteed polynomial and complete resolver would solve an NP-complete problem in polynomial time. Practical tools use CDCL SAT solvers, which handle most real repositories quickly but have no worst-case guarantee.

options.text: Restrict the resolver to the first 10 packages to keep it polynomial
options.explanation: Truncating the input doesn't solve the problem; it just gives wrong answers on larger installs.

options.text: NP-complete problems can't be solved at all, so drop version constraints
options.explanation: NP-complete problems are decidable and often solvable in practice. Throwing away constraints breaks correctness.

Encode version choices and dependency/conflict rules for a SAT solver instead, and measure it on the workload. Preserve all constraints, set a deadline and distinguish timeout from a proven no-answer. Good typical performance is not a universal polynomial-time guarantee.

lessons.title: Intermediate problems and numeric hardness
lessons.summary: Ladner’s theorem gives NP-intermediate problems if P differs from NP.
lessons.body:
## Not everything is P or NP-complete

**Ladner's theorem (1975)**: if P and NP are different, there are problems in NP that are neither in P nor NP-complete (**NP-intermediate**).

The theorem's examples are artificial. Natural candidates include bounded-factor decision and graph isomorphism, but nobody can prove them intermediate, because a problem in NP but not in P would itself prove that P and NP differ.

**Weak versus strong.** Subset sum and knapsack are NP-complete with unrestricted binary numbers, while a polynomial bound on their values makes their pseudo-polynomial DP polynomial-time. This is a statement about restricted input families, not a claim every large-number instance is difficult. They are *weakly* NP-complete. Problems like 3-partition and TSP stay NP-complete even when numeric values have a polynomial bound in input length: *strongly* NP-complete.

## Key takeaways

- Ladner’s theorem gives NP-intermediate problems if P differs from NP.
- Factoring decision and graph isomorphism are candidates, not proven intermediate problems.
- Weak and strong NP-completeness distinguish whether small numeric bounds remove hardness.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Theory of Computation — MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/)

questions.prompt: Suppose someone proved that graph isomorphism is **NP-intermediate** (in NP, not in P, not NP-complete). What would follow?

options.text: Nothing new; Ladner's theorem already says it
options.explanation: Ladner's theorem is conditional: *if* P differs from NP then intermediate problems exist. It doesn't name graph isomorphism or any natural problem.

options.text: P equals NP
options.explanation: If P equals NP, every NP problem would be in P, so nothing could be 'in NP but not in P'.

options.text: P differs from NP
options.explanation: Correct. A problem in NP but not in P immediately separates the two classes. This is why no natural problem has been proven NP-intermediate.

options.text: Graph isomorphism is undecidable
options.explanation: It's decidable (try every one-to-one matching between the two graphs' vertices) and in NP. Intermediate refers to complexity, not decidability.

questions.workedExample: NP-intermediate explicitly includes membership in NP and non-membership in P. A single such problem would separate the classes. Ladner’s theorem instead starts by assuming the separation and proves that intermediate problems would exist; it does not identify graph isomorphism as one.

questions.prompt: Subset sum is NP-complete. Which of these statements are correct? Select all that apply. Assume nonnegative subset-sum inputs; n is the number of input numbers.

options.text: If every number in the input is at most the square of the item count, subset sum can be solved in polynomial time
options.explanation: Correct. The sum of all nonnegative items then has a polynomial bound too. Reject targets above that sum; the remaining dynamic-programming table has polynomial width.

options.text: The previous fact contradicts subset sum being NP-complete
options.explanation: Restricting every value to a polynomial bound defines an easier input family. General binary-encoded inputs do not have that restriction; this does not classify each large-value instance as hard.

options.text: TSP stays NP-complete even when every edge weight is 1 or 2
options.explanation: Correct. Hamiltonian cycle reduces to it: give graph edges weight 1, non-edges weight 2, and ask for a tour of cost at most the number of vertices. This is why TSP is called strongly NP-complete.

options.text: Knapsack has a pseudo-polynomial algorithm
options.explanation: Correct. The knapsack DP, whose cost is the number of items times the capacity W, is polynomial when W is written in unary or otherwise polynomially bounded in the encoded instance length; arbitrary binary W may be exponential.

options.text: Strongly NP-complete problems have pseudo-polynomial algorithms unless P equals NP
options.explanation: Reversed: a strongly NP-complete problem has no pseudo-polynomial algorithm unless P equals NP.

questions.workedExample: With nonnegative items, a target above their total is immediately impossible. If every item value has a polynomial bound in the item count, the total and useful table width do too. This restricted family is therefore tractable without contradicting general binary Subset Sum hardness. TSP remains hard even with weights one and two, so bounding its numeric values does not remove hardness.

lessons.title: Using a map of reductions
lessons.summary: A reduction transfers hardness from its source to its target.
lessons.body:
Cook–Levin gives us one NP-complete problem the hard way. Every other NP-completeness proof is a **polynomial-time reduction**: a recipe that turns instances of a known hard problem into instances of the new one, preserving the yes/no answer.

Designing reductions is a craft. The usual approach is to build **gadgets**: small pieces of the target problem that imitate a variable ("choose true or false") or a constraint ("at least one of these must hold").

## The reduction map

```
        SAT
         |   (CNF + clause splitting)
       3-SAT
      /  |   \
     IS  3-COL SUBSET-SUM
    / \          |
  VC  CLIQUE   KNAPSACK
   |
 SET-COVER   (and many more)
```

An arrow from a source problem to a target means a polynomial-time translation preserves both yes and no answers. A fast target solver would therefore solve the source too. The direction transfers hardness forwards and algorithms backwards.

So once A is NP-hard, every problem below it on the map is NP-hard too. For example, 3-SAT reduces to IS (Independent Set), and IS reduces to VC (Vertex Cover), so VC is NP-hard.

## Key takeaways

- A reduction transfers hardness from its source to its target.
- Gadgets represent choices and constraints inside a target problem.
- Arrows in the reduction map preserve the yes/no answer.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

questions.prompt: An arrow runs from 3-SAT to Independent Set in a polynomial-time reduction map. What would a polynomial-time Independent Set decision algorithm provide?

options.text: A polynomial-time algorithm for 3-SAT by translating first
options.explanation: Correct. Translate the formula, then run the target solver; answer preservation gives a solver for the source.

options.text: Only a way to solve Independent Set on satisfiable formulas
options.explanation: The reduction works for both yes- and no-instances, without knowing satisfiability beforehand.

options.text: A proof that 3-SAT is not in NP
options.explanation: 3-SAT has polynomially checkable assignments, so it is in NP.

options.text: A proof that no algorithm for 3-SAT can exist
options.explanation: The reduction transfers algorithms; it does not establish an unconditional lower bound.

questions.workedExample:
1. Translate the input formula into a graph and target size.
2. Run the assumed polynomial-time target decision algorithm.
3. Return its answer: the reduction preserves both yes and no, so this decides 3-SAT in polynomial time.

lessons.title: Building clause and consistency gadgets
lessons.summary: Independent sets have no internal edges and are easy to verify.
lessons.body:
## 3-SAT to Independent Set

**Independent Set (IS)**: given a graph G and integer k, is there a set of k vertices with no edge between any two of them? A larger independent set also contains one of exactly the requested size.

IS is in NP: the certificate lists the selected vertices. Check that they are distinct valid vertices and that no selected pair is an edge. There are only quadratically many pairs, so this is polynomial work.

Now the reduction. It starts from a **3-CNF formula** φ: an AND of m clauses, where each clause is an OR of exactly 3 **literals** (a variable such as x or its negation ¬x). Given φ:

1. **Clause gadget.** For each clause, create 3 vertices, one per literal, joined in a **graph triangle**. An independent set can take at most one vertex per triangle: it "picks the literal that satisfies this clause".
2. **Consistency edges.** Join every vertex labelled x to every vertex labelled ¬x, in any clause. You can't pick x in one clause and ¬x in another.
3. Set the target size **k** equal to the number of clauses **m**.

Every literal occurrence gets its own vertex, even when the same literal appears elsewhere. The target counts clauses, not distinct variables: reaching it forces exactly one choice from each triangle.

## Key takeaways

- Independent sets have no internal edges and are easy to verify.
- Each clause becomes a triangle of literal occurrences.
- Consistency edges forbid complementary literals; the target equals the clause count.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

options.text: Each variable can be selected only once
options.explanation: Vertices represent occurrences; compatible occurrences of the same literal can be selected in different clauses.

options.text: At most one pick per triangle plus that target forces every clause to contribute
options.explanation: This gives a chosen literal in each clause, which is essential to reconstructing a satisfying assignment.

options.text: The graph contains one vertex per variable
options.explanation: It contains one vertex per literal occurrence.

options.text: A smaller target always proves unsatisfiability
options.explanation: A smaller target can ignore clauses, so its success need not imply satisfiability.

questions.workedExample: A triangle permits at most one selected occurrence from its clause. Asking for as many selected vertices as clauses therefore forces a pick from every triangle. Counting distinct variables instead could allow the algorithm to skip clauses, breaking the inference from an independent set to a satisfying assignment.

options.text: A satisfying assignment must now create an edge between its true picks
options.explanation: Removing an edge cannot invalidate an independent set that previously worked.

options.text: Selected literals may no longer extend to a consistent truth assignment
options.explanation: Opposite occurrences can now both be selected, so graph choices need not describe one assignment.

options.text: Two vertices from the same triangle can be picked
options.explanation: Triangle edges are still present and forbid that.

options.text: The graph is too large to construct in polynomial time
options.explanation: Omitting an edge changes correctness, not the polynomial size bound.
