Without the edge between a positive occurrence and a negative occurrence of the same variable, both could be selected. Each clause triangle still limits local picks, but the selections may not extend to one global assignment.

lessons.title: Tracing a SAT-to-graph instance
lessons.summary: Choose compatible literal occurrences to translate between an assignment and an independent set.
lessons.body:
### A worked instance

Here is a formula with three clauses over four Boolean variables:

```formula essential
φ = (x1 ∨ x2 ∨ ¬x3)
  ∧ (¬x1 ∨ x3 ∨ x4)
  ∧ (¬x2 ∨ ¬x3 ∨ ¬x4)
where
φ: phi, the whole 3-CNF formula; it is true when every bracketed clause is true
x1, x2, x3, x4: Boolean variables, each set to true or false
¬: NOT: ¬x3 is true exactly when x3 is false
∨: OR: a clause is true when at least one of its 3 literals is true
∧: AND: joins the clauses; φ is true only when all of them are true
In words: three clauses, C1, C2 and C3 in order; φ is satisfiable if some true/false setting of x1 to x4 makes at least one literal true in every clause.
```

```
 C1:   x1 ---- x2       C2:  ¬x1 ---- x3
         \    /                \     /
          ¬x3                    x4

 C3:  ¬x2 ---- ¬x3
         \     /
          ¬x4

 consistency edges (5):
  C1.x1  -- C2.¬x1    C1.x2  -- C3.¬x2
  C1.¬x3 -- C2.x3     C2.x3  -- C3.¬x3
  C2.x4  -- C3.¬x4
```

The graph has nine vertices, one per occurrence, and target size three. Triangle edges enforce one choice per clause; the five listed consistency edges prevent contradictory choices.

Set the first and third variables true and the second false (the fourth can be anything). The first clause is satisfied by the first variable, the second by the third variable, and the last by the negation of the second variable.

Pick one true literal from each clause: x1 from C1, x3 from C2, ¬x2 from C3. These three vertices are in different triangles, and no two are complementary, so they form an independent set of size 3.

## Key takeaways

- Triangle edges enforce clause choices; consistency edges forbid contradictory choices.
- Choose a true literal from each clause to obtain an independent set.
- Picked nonconflicting literals can be extended to an assignment.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

where
φ: phi, the whole formula; its three bracketed clauses are C1, C2, C3 in order
x1, x2, x3, x4: Boolean variables, each true or false
∨: OR: a clause is true when at least one literal is true
∧: AND: every clause must be true
¬: NOT: ¬x3 is true exactly when x3 is false
In words: three clauses that must all hold, each with three literals.

Every clause has a chosen true literal, so the first variable can be either value. This is the graph-to-assignment direction on a concrete instance.

lessons.title: Executing and proving the graph reduction
lessons.summary: The executable construction uses a vertex per occurrence.
lessons.body:
Use the same construction as the preceding units: one triangle per three-literal clause, consistency edges between complementary occurrences, and a target equal to the number of clauses. In the code, a positive integer represents a variable and a negative integer its negation.

### Checking it in Python

```python
from itertools import combinations

def sat_to_is(phi):
    # vertex = (clause, position, literal)
    V = [(i, j, l)
         for i, c in enumerate(phi)
         for j, l in enumerate(c)]
    # Edges forbid same-clause or opposite
    # picks.
    E = set()
    for u, v in combinations(V, 2):
        same = u[0] == v[0]
        clash = u[2] == -v[2]
        if same or clash:
            E.add((u, v))
    return V, E, len(phi)

def has_is(V, E, k):
    # Exhaustive search is only for tiny
    # audits.
    for S in combinations(V, k):
        if not any((u, v) in E for u, v
                   in combinations(S, 2)):
            return S
    return None

phi = [[1, 2, -3], [-1, 3, 4], [-2, -3, -4]]
V, E, k = sat_to_is(phi)
print(len(V), len(E), k)   # 9 14 3
print(has_is(V, E, k))
# ((0, 0, 1), (1, 1, 3), (2, 0, -2))
```

Literals are integers: 3 means x3, −3 means ¬x3. The independent set found is exactly x1 from C1, x3 from C2 and ¬x2 from C3.

For a no-instance, take all eight sign patterns over three distinct variables. Every assignment falsifies one clause. The construction therefore cannot have an independent set taking one vertex from every clause. Exhaustive tests can check this small case, but the two-direction proof below establishes correctness for all inputs.

### Why it's correct (both directions)

The claim has two directions: the formula is satisfiable exactly when the graph has an independent set whose size equals the clause count.

Each direction, and the running time:

- **If φ is satisfiable, there is an independent set of size m.** Fix a satisfying assignment. Each clause has a true literal; pick its vertex. One per triangle, so no triangle edges. All picked literals are true, so none is the negation of another, so no consistency edges. Size m.
- **If there is an independent set of size m, φ is satisfiable.** At most one vertex per triangle, and there are m triangles, so exactly one per clause. No consistency edge is inside the set, so the picked literals never include both x and ¬x. Set those literals true (others arbitrarily). Every clause has a true literal.
- **Polynomial.** Each clause creates three vertices. Checking each pair creates at most quadratically many edges in the clause count, so the construction is polynomial.

> [!tip] Gadget pattern
> Triangles enforce "choose exactly one" (given a budget of one vertex per clause). Edges between conflicting choices enforce consistency. You'll see this pattern again and again.

More generally, an assignment satisfying a given number of clauses provides an independent set of that size by choosing one true occurrence per satisfied clause. Conversely, any independent set extends to a consistent assignment satisfying every clause represented by a picked vertex. Thus the maximum independent-set size equals the maximum number of simultaneously satisfiable clauses; for all eight sign patterns on three variables, that number is seven.

## Key takeaways

- The executable construction uses a vertex per occurrence.
- Both directions of the proof are necessary for a valid reduction.
- Exhaustive checks illustrate the result on finite examples; the proof covers all instances.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

lessons.title: Independent sets, covers and cliques
lessons.summary: Complementing a vertex set exchanges independent sets and covers.
lessons.body:
Continue with finite simple undirected graphs. Exact reductions connect three different graph questions; their decision thresholds use at least the requested independent/clique size and at most the requested cover size. A set of exactly the target independent size exists whenever a larger one does.

## Independent Set, Vertex Cover and Clique

A **vertex cover** is a set C of vertices touching every edge: every edge has at least one end in C. The key observation links it to independent sets:

```formula essential
S ∈ I(G)  iff  (V ∖ S) ∈ C(G)
f(G, k) = (G, n − k)
where
S: any set of vertices of the graph G
I(G): the collection of all independent sets of G (vertex sets with no edge inside them)
C(G): the collection of all vertex covers of G (vertex sets touching every edge)
∈: "is a member of"
G: the input graph, with vertex set V
V: the set of all vertices of G
∖: set difference: V ∖ S is every vertex of V that is not in S
n: the number of vertices in G
k: the independent-set size asked for
f: the reduction from Independent Set to Vertex Cover
f(G, k): the Vertex Cover instance it outputs: the same graph, with target size n − k
In words: a set is independent exactly when the vertices left over touch every edge, so asking for an independent set of size k is the same as asking for a vertex cover of size n − k.
```

Why the first line holds: if no edge has both ends in S, every edge has at least one end outside S, and vice versa. So the reduction doesn't even change the graph; it only changes the number. Increasing the independent set removes vertices from its complementary cover. A maximum independent set therefore leaves a minimum cover.

A **clique** is a set of vertices all joined to each other. S is independent in G exactly when S is a clique in the **complement** graph Ḡ (same vertices, edges exactly where G has none). Retain the target size and build the complement by examining each pair of distinct vertices: polynomial work.

```
 G: 1-2, 2-3        complement: 1-3
 {1,3} independent  {1,3} a clique
 {2} covers both edges of G
```

An exhaustive audit checks the IS/VC equivalence for every vertex subset of every simple five-vertex graph. The complement argument above establishes the general statement.

For these decision maps the target is a nonnegative integer no larger than the vertex count. Out-of-range or malformed target encodings can be handled separately by a fixed yes- or no-instance as appropriate. The complement graph has no self-loops and considers only pairs of distinct vertices.

## Key takeaways

- Complementing a vertex set exchanges independent sets and covers.
- Complementing graph edges exchanges independent sets and cliques.
- The transformations run in polynomial time.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

lessons.title: Why exact reductions need not preserve ratios
lessons.summary: Exact decision equivalence does not ensure approximation equivalence.
lessons.body:
The preceding exact maps connect Independent Set, Vertex Cover and Clique. Approximation additionally asks how a returned feasible solution compares with the optimum. For an objective where lower cost is better, factor two means a cost at most twice optimum; for maximisation it means a value at least half optimum.

Vertex Cover has a polynomial-time factor-two approximation. Complementing the returned cover still produces a valid independent set, but its quality can be arbitrarily poor. If the optimum cover uses half the vertices, a factor-two algorithm may legally return every vertex. Its complement is empty even though a large independent set exists.

For Clique and Independent Set, polynomial-time approximation within a factor equal to any fixed positive power of vertex count below one is NP-hard. This is a worst-case, asymptotic statement under the assumption that P differs from NP.

Exact reductions preserve answers or optimum values in a specified way. Transferring an approximation additionally requires controlling how solution errors change; subtraction from the vertex count can destroy a multiplicative guarantee.

## Key takeaways

- Exact decision equivalence does not ensure approximation equivalence.
- A factor-two cover can leave an empty independent-set complement.
- Clique and independent set have much worse polynomial-time approximation limits.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

options.explanation: The 2-approximation can return up to 1,000 vertices, whose complement is empty. Nothing like 250 is guaranteed.

options.text: An independent set of size at least 500
options.explanation: That would need an exact minimum cover; the approximation only promises at most 1,000.

options.text: Nothing useful: the cover may have up to 1,000 vertices, leaving an independent set of size 0
options.explanation: Correct. Exact reductions preserve yes/no answers, not approximation ratios. A factor-2 error on n − k becomes an unbounded error on k.

options.text: An independent set within a factor 2 of the maximum
options.explanation: Subtracting an approximate cover size from the vertex count does not preserve a multiplicative approximation ratio.

questions.workedExample: A factor-two cover may include every vertex when the optimum cover includes half of them. Its complement is a valid independent set but can be empty, despite a large optimum independent set. The exact complement relationship survives; the multiplicative quality guarantee does not.

lessons.title: Edges as elements and numeric reductions
lessons.summary: Vertex Cover reduces to Set Cover with edges as elements.
lessons.body:
## Vertex Cover to Set Cover

**Set Cover**: given a universe U, a family of subsets, and k, can at most k of the subsets cover all of U?

From a Vertex Cover instance (G, k), build a Set Cover instance:

```formula essential
U = E
S_v = { {v, w} ∈ E }
k_SC = k
where
U: the universe: the set of elements that must all be covered
E: the set of edges of the graph G
G: the input graph of the Vertex Cover instance
v: any vertex of G; there is one set per vertex
S_v: the set of edges that touch vertex v (the edges incident to v)
w: any other vertex joined to v by an edge, so {v, w} is an edge with v at one end
∈: "is a member of"
k: the vertex cover size asked for
k_SC: the count of subsets in the family the Set Cover instance may use
In words: the elements to cover are the edges, and each vertex becomes the set of edges it touches. Choosing k vertices that touch every edge is exactly choosing k sets that cover every element.
```

Set Cover is in NP because a chosen family can be checked by taking its union. Combined with this reduction, Set Cover is therefore NP-complete, and Vertex Cover is the special case where every element (edge) is in exactly two sets. For a star with centre 0 and leaves 1 to 4, U holds the 4 edges, there are 5 sets, and the centre's set alone covers U, matching the vertex cover {0}.

## Other classic reductions, briefly

- **3-SAT to 3-colouring.** A "palette" triangle with colours TRUE, FALSE, BASE; each variable is an edge x–¬x joined to BASE (so one is TRUE, one FALSE); each clause is a small OR-gadget that can be properly coloured only if at least one of its literals is TRUE.
- **3-SAT to Subset Sum.** Each literal and clause becomes a large decimal number with one digit column per variable and per clause, so that hitting the target forces one choice per variable and at least one true literal per clause. The numbers have one digit per variable and per clause so the written length remains polynomial. Its pseudo-polynomial algorithm, discussed below, makes the distinction between numeric value and encoding length important.
- **Hamiltonian cycle to TSP.** Edges weight 1, non-edges weight 2, and a tour-length budget equal to the number of vertices.

The Subset Sum numbers are short to write but can be huge in value. With one digit per variable and clause, the digit count grows linearly while the possible values grow exponentially. Binary and decimal encodings differ by only a constant factor in length.

The reduction is polynomial because it writes compact positional encodings. Subset Sum’s dynamic program instead has a column per possible target value; that table can be exponentially wider than the written input. If all values are polynomially bounded, the useful targets are too, and the dynamic program becomes polynomial. This is why Subset Sum is called weakly NP-complete. The reduction alone is not a proof that small-number instances are easy.

## Key takeaways

- Vertex Cover reduces to Set Cover with edges as elements.
- Literal and clause gadgets also encode colouring and subset sum.
- Huge numeric values are compatible with polynomial-size binary encodings.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

options.explanation: The universe consists of edges, not vertices.

options.text: Every edge touches the centre
options.explanation: Its incident-edge set contains every universe element, matching the one-vertex graph cover.

options.explanation: A leaf touches only its own edge.

options.explanation: Every universe element must be covered, just as every graph edge must be touched.

lessons.title: Checking direction, size and reduction type
lessons.summary: A valid reduction must be polynomial and preserve answers in both directions.
lessons.body:
## Pitfalls that invalidate a reduction

1. **Wrong direction.** To show X is hard, map *from* the known hard problem *to* X.
2. **Only one direction proved.** You need both directions: every yes-instance must map to a yes-instance, *and* every instance that maps to a yes-instance must itself be a yes-instance (equivalently, no-instances map to no-instances). Many broken proofs show only that satisfying assignments give solutions.
3. **Using the answer.** The reduction can't "first find a satisfying assignment". It must run in polynomial time without solving the problem.
4. **Exponential blow-up.** Encoding every possible assignment, or writing numbers in unary, breaks polynomial time.
5. **Forgetting membership.** Hardness plus a reduction gives NP-hard; you still need to show X is in NP to claim NP-complete.

> [!note] Karp versus Cook reductions
> Everything here is a **many-one (Karp)** reduction: one call to B, answer passed through unchanged. A **Turing (Cook)** reduction may call B many times and post-process. Turing reductions are more powerful; for example, they make SAT and UNSAT reduce to each other trivially, which blurs NP versus coNP. NP-completeness is standardly defined with Karp reductions.

## Key takeaways

- A valid reduction must be polynomial and preserve answers in both directions.
- The construction cannot assume a solution to the source problem.
- Karp reductions pass through one answer; Cook reductions may adapt and negate answers.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

questions.prompt: Which of these are valid polynomial-time many-one reductions? Select all that apply.

options.text: Independent Set to Vertex Cover: keep the graph and subtract the requested independent size from the vertex count
options.explanation: Valid. A set is independent exactly when the remaining vertices form a cover.

options.text: Independent Set to Clique: complement the graph and retain the target size
options.explanation: Valid. Independent sets of G are cliques of the complement graph, built with one check per pair of vertices (about n²/2 for n vertices).

options.text: 3-SAT to IS: enumerate every assignment with brute force; then output a fixed yes-instance or no-instance
options.explanation: The yes/no result is preserved, but enumerating all assignments is exponential in the variable count, so the stated construction is not a polynomial-time reduction.

options.text: Vertex Cover to Set Cover: use edges as elements and one incident-edge set per vertex, retaining the budget
options.explanation: Valid. Some k vertices touch every edge exactly when their k sets cover every element.

options.text: Subset Sum to Unary Subset Sum: rewrite each number in unary
options.explanation: Invalid. A number written in b bits can be as large as about 2 to the power b, and unary encoding needs that many symbols, so the output is exponentially larger than the input.

questions.workedExample: The first two graph transformations preserve the answer and require only polynomial work. Edges-as-elements does too: selecting a vertex corresponds exactly to selecting its incident-edge set. Brute-force solving before translating is not polynomial, and rewriting a binary number in unary can require exponentially much output. Answer preservation alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: A paper claims "SCHEDULE is NP-complete" with this proof: (1) a schedule is a certificate checkable in polynomial time; (2) we give a polynomial-time reduction from SCHEDULE to 3-SAT. What has actually been proven?

options.text: SCHEDULE is NP-complete, as claimed
options.explanation: Step (2) is in the wrong direction. A reduction from SCHEDULE to 3-SAT says 3-SAT can solve SCHEDULE, which is true for every NP problem.

options.text: Only that SCHEDULE is in NP
options.explanation: Correct. Step (1) proves membership in NP, and step (2) adds nothing new, since everything in NP reduces to 3-SAT by Cook–Levin. NP-hardness needs a reduction the other way, from 3-SAT to SCHEDULE.

options.text: SCHEDULE is NP-hard but maybe not in NP
options.explanation: Nothing in the argument establishes hardness.

options.text: SCHEDULE is in P
options.explanation: No algorithm for SCHEDULE has been given; reducing to 3-SAT gives only an exponential-time algorithm (via brute-force SAT).

questions.workedExample: The verifier proves SCHEDULE is in NP. Translating SCHEDULE to 3-SAT only shows a SAT solver could solve it, something already true of NP problems. To transfer hardness to SCHEDULE, the proof needs a polynomial-time answer-preserving translation from a known hard problem into SCHEDULE.

questions.prompt: Many-one (Karp) versus Turing (Cook) reductions. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Under Turing reductions, UNSAT reduces to SAT trivially: call SAT once and negate the answer
options.explanation: Correct. Turing reductions may post-process the oracle's answer, so complements are free.

options.text: If UNSAT many-one reduces to SAT in polynomial time, then NP equals coNP
options.explanation: Correct. A Karp reduction would put UNSAT in NP; UNSAT is coNP-complete, so every coNP problem would be in NP, and hence NP and coNP would be equal.

options.text: NP-completeness is standardly defined using Karp reductions
options.explanation: Correct. Using Turing reductions would make NP and coNP problems equally 'complete', erasing a distinction we believe is real.

options.text: A Turing reduction may call the target problem at most once
options.explanation: That's the many-one restriction. Turing reductions may make polynomially many adaptive calls.

options.text: Karp reductions are more powerful than Turing reductions
options.explanation: Backwards. Every Karp reduction is a Turing reduction with one call and no post-processing, so Turing reductions are at least as powerful.

questions.workedExample: A Turing reduction may negate SAT’s answer, immediately deciding UNSAT. A many-one reduction must preserve the answer without that negation. If UNSAT many-one reduced to SAT, a satisfying assignment to the translated formula would certify unsatisfiability of the original, putting UNSAT in NP and collapsing NP with coNP. Karp reductions retain that distinction.

lessons.title: Special structure and smarter exact search
lessons.summary: Restricted instances can have polynomial-time exact algorithms.
lessons.body:
Proving a problem NP-hard doesn't make it go away. Airlines still need crew rosters, chip designers still need verified circuits, and delivery firms still need routes. NP-hardness tells you that you can't have all three of these at once, assuming the widely believed conjecture below:

1. **Exact** answers,
2. on **every** input,
3. in **polynomial** time.

The assumption is that P and NP are different: short checkable certificates do not always imply a polynomial-time solving algorithm. This remains unproven.

Every coping strategy gives up one of the three properties. This lesson works through the options, with the guarantees each one does and doesn't give.

## Option 1: your inputs may be a special case

Hard problems often become easy on restricted inputs. Check before anything else.

| Problem | Hard in general | Easy when |
|---|---|---|
| Vertex cover | Any graph | Bipartite (matching) |
| Independent set | Any graph | Trees (DP) |
| SAT | 3-CNF | 2-CNF, Horn |
| Colouring | 3 colours | 2 colours |

More generally, many NP-hard graph problems are solvable in linear time on graphs of bounded **treewidth** (Courcelle's theorem), with constants that grow very fast in the width.

## Option 2: exact, but exponential and smarter

Exponential is not one speed. Take the travelling salesperson problem (TSP) on n cities. For symmetric TSP on at least three cities, brute force fixes a starting city, tries every order of the other n − 1 cities, and halves the count because each closed tour can be driven in two directions. The **Held–Karp** dynamic program (1962) instead builds the best path through every subset of cities, which costs far less:

```formula reference
N_tours = (n − 1)! / 2
T_HK = O(n^2 2^n)
where
N_tours: the number of different closed tours brute force must try
n: the number of cities
!: factorial: m! = m × (m − 1) × … × 2 × 1, the number of ways to put m things in order
T_HK: the number of basic steps Held–Karp takes
O(...): Big O: grows at most as fast as a constant times the expression inside, for large n
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together; here, the number of subsets of the n cities
In words: enumerating tours has factorial growth. Held–Karp instead has an exponential subset factor multiplied by a polynomial in the city count. Reusing subproblems improves growth dramatically, but the subset factor remains exponential.
```

The important gain is reuse: many candidate tours share the same “visited cities and last city” subproblem. Held–Karp solves that subproblem once. The number of subsets is still exponential, so the method remains unsuitable for large unrestricted instances. Its asymptotic bound is not a measured operation count.

Industrial exact methods go much further using **branch and bound** and cutting planes: prove a lower bound for a whole region of the search space and skip it if it can't beat the best answer so far. The Concorde TSP solver found and proved the optimal tour for an 85,900-city instance in 2006. MIP solvers for integer programming (Gurobi, CPLEX, HiGHS) combine branching, bounds and cuts. CDCL SAT solvers also search and prune, but use learned logical conflict clauses rather than the same numeric optimisation bounds.

## Key takeaways

- Restricted instances can have polynomial-time exact algorithms.
- Held–Karp replaces factorial enumeration with subset dynamic programming.
- Exact solvers prune search using valid bounds while retaining correctness.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

options.text: A polynomial-time exact algorithm for all TSP inputs
options.explanation: There are still exponentially many subsets.

options.text: Reuse of shared subproblems, with an exponential subset cost remaining
options.explanation: It avoids recomputing many common prefixes but does not remove exponential growth.

There are still exponentially many subsets. The improvement changes the growth substantially but does not give a polynomial-time exact algorithm.

lessons.title: A matching gives a two-approximation
lessons.summary: Approximation gives up exactness while keeping a quality guarantee.
lessons.body:
## Option 3: approximation algorithms

An approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time and always returns a solution that is provably close to the best one. The closeness is measured by a factor α:

```formula reference
ALG_min ≤ α OPT_min
ALG_max ≥ OPT_max / α
where
ALG_min: the cost of the solution the algorithm returns, for a problem where lower cost is better (lower is better, e.g. a route length)
OPT_min: the cost of the best possible solution to the same input
ALG_max: the value the algorithm achieves, for a maximisation problem (higher is better, e.g. clauses satisfied)
OPT_max: the best possible value for the same input
α: alpha, the approximation factor, at least 1; it may depend on input size, and α = 1 means always optimal
In words: the approximation factor limits how far a feasible answer can be from optimum. Factor two means at most twice optimum cost for minimisation, or at least half optimum value for maximisation.
```

For nonnegative minimisation costs, factor two means at most twice the optimum cost; for maximisation it means at least half the optimum value. The algorithm must return a feasible solution. The guarantee holds on every permitted input, without knowing the optimum. Some authors write maximisation guarantees as a factor below 1 instead (for example "0.5-approximation" for the same thing as 2 here), so check the convention.

### Vertex cover: a 2-approximation in five lines

A vertex cover is a set of vertices that touches every edge. Repeatedly take an edge with neither end covered, and add **both** endpoints.

```python
def vc_2approx(edges):
    cover = set()
    for u, v in edges:
        # Pick only edges disjoint from past
        # picks.
        if not ({u, v} & cover):
            cover |= {u, v}
    return cover

path = [(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)]
print(vc_2approx(path))   # {1, 2, 3, 4}
# optimum is {2, 3}: ratio exactly 2
```

Why it's within factor 2: the edges we picked form a **graph matching** M (no two share a vertex). Any cover, including the optimal one, must contain at least one endpoint of each matched edge, and those endpoints are all different. That gives a lower bound on the optimum and an exact count for our cover:

```formula essential
OPT ≥ |M|
|C| = 2|M|
|C| = 2|M| ≤ 2OPT
where
M: the matching: the edges the algorithm picked, no two sharing a vertex
|M|: the number of edges in M
OPT: the size (number of vertices) of a smallest vertex cover
C: the cover the algorithm returns; |C| is its number of vertices
In words: every cover needs a different vertex for each picked edge, so the best cover has at least |M| vertices. The algorithm takes exactly two per picked edge, so it is never more than twice the best.
```

The path example shows the bound is tight: the algorithm picks the first and last edges, which form a two-edge matching, and returns four vertices. The two middle vertices cover all three edges, so the minimum cover has size two and the approximation ratio is exactly two. An exhaustive finite audit compares the algorithm with optimum covers on every simple graph with up to five vertices; all returned sets cover every edge and satisfy the factor-two bound. The matching proof gives the guarantee for arbitrary simple graphs.

## Key takeaways

- Approximation gives up exactness while keeping a quality guarantee.
- Taking both ends of uncovered edges builds a cover from a matching.
- Every cover needs one distinct endpoint per matched edge, proving the factor two.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [The Design of Approximation Algorithms — Williamson and Shmoys](https://www.designofapproxalgs.com/book.pdf)

questions.prompt: Assuming P and NP are different classes (the standard conjecture), an NP-hard optimisation problem can't be solved exactly, on every input, in polynomial time. A **2-approximation algorithm** for it gives up which of those three properties?

options.text: Polynomial time
options.explanation: Approximation algorithms are required to run in polynomial time; that's the whole point of them.

options.text: Working on every input
options.explanation: An approximation guarantee holds on every input. Heuristics are the ones that give up worst-case guarantees.

options.text: Exactness: it returns a solution guaranteed within a factor 2 of optimal
options.explanation: Correct. It gives up exactness while retaining polynomial running time and an all-input quality bound: at most twice optimum cost for a nonnegative minimisation objective, or at least half optimum for maximisation.

options.text: None; it beats NP-hardness
options.explanation: If it gave up nothing, it would solve the problem exactly in polynomial time, which would mean P and NP are the same class.

questions.workedExample: Approximation keeps polynomial running time and a guarantee on every permitted input, but allows a feasible answer that is not optimal. A factor-two minimisation guarantee permits up to twice the optimum cost. It therefore relaxes exactness without contradicting the assumed hardness of finding the exact optimum.

questions.prompt: In the proof that the matching algorithm is a 2-approximation for vertex cover, why is OPT (the size of a smallest vertex cover) at least |M|, where M is the set of edges the algorithm picked and |M| is how many there are?

options.text: Because the algorithm's cover has size 2|M|
options.explanation: That's the size of *our* cover. The lower bound on OPT needs a separate argument about every possible cover.

options.text: Because the edges in M share no endpoints, and any cover must include at least one endpoint of each, so it needs |M| distinct vertices

lessons.title: Approximation schemes and representative limits
lessons.summary: Guarantees and hardness limits vary widely by problem and metric assumptions.
lessons.body:
### A spectrum of approximability

Approximation quality depends on the problem and its assumptions. A factor near one is strong; a factor that grows with input size becomes weaker on larger instances. These are representative results, not a list of current records.

| Problem | Available guarantee | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Knapsack | Chosen relative accuracy | FPTAS trades time for accuracy |
| Symmetric metric TSP | Factor 1.5; slight improvements known | No PTAS unless P equals NP |
| Vertex Cover | Factor two | No PTAS unless P equals NP |
| Unweighted Set Cover | Factor logarithmic in universe size | Near-logarithmic hardness |
| General TSP | No constant factor unless P equals NP | Metric assumptions matter |
| Clique | Much weaker size-dependent bounds | Near-linear factor hardness |

For example, the knapsack FPTAS can guarantee at least 99 percent of optimum value. It rounds item values and runs dynamic programming on the rounded values, reducing the table size while controlling the loss. Tighter accuracy requires more work.

For symmetric metric TSP, distances are nonnegative and obey the triangle inequality. Christofides gives factor 1.5; published work improves that bound slightly. General TSP allows arbitrary nonnegative weights, so a construction with expensive non-edges can defeat every fixed constant guarantee.

Greedy unweighted set cover repeatedly picks the set that covers most uncovered elements. Its guarantee grows logarithmically in the number of elements. Exact numeric thresholds are useful references, but the choice here is whether the problem admits freely adjustable accuracy or a barrier prevents it.

A PTAS is polynomial for each fixed accuracy; its input-size exponent may depend on that accuracy. An FPTAS is polynomial jointly in input length and inverse accuracy. For knapsack, first discard items heavier than the capacity. The largest remaining single-item value is then at most the optimum, so rounding each value down loses less than one rounding step per selected item. Choosing the step as the allowed error times that largest feasible value divided by the item count limits the total loss to the allowed fraction of the optimum. Zero-value or empty feasible instances are trivial.

For integer objective values polynomially bounded in input length, choosing relative error smaller than the reciprocal of that bound makes the allowed additive loss less than one. An FPTAS must then return the exact integer optimum in polynomial time. This rules out an FPTAS for the stated hard families unless P equals NP.

## Key takeaways

- Guarantees and hardness limits vary widely by problem and metric assumptions.
- Knapsack has an FPTAS with runtime polynomial in input length and inverse accuracy.
- A PTAS for an APX-hard problem would imply P equals NP.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Deterministic metric TSP improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.06296)
- [The Design of Approximation Algorithms — Williamson and Shmoys](https://www.designofapproxalgs.com/book.pdf)
- [Metric TSP hardness — Karpinski, Lampis and Schmied](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.6437)

options.text: Knapsack has an FPTAS: it supports any chosen positive relative-error tolerance, with time polynomial in the input length and the inverse tolerance
options.explanation: Correct. Round item values while controlling the total loss, then run the pseudo-polynomial dynamic program on those smaller values.

options.text: Metric TSP has a PTAS
options.explanation: It's APX-hard: approximating below 123/122 is NP-hard, so no PTAS exists unless P equals NP. (Euclidean TSP, a special case, does have one: Arora, 1998.)

options.text: A strongly NP-hard problem with polynomially bounded nonnegative integer objective values has no FPTAS unless P equals NP
options.explanation: Correct. Choose ε smaller than one over the largest possible objective value; the FPTAS's error is then less than 1, so on integers it must return the exact optimum in polynomial time.

options.text: An FPTAS returns the exact optimum in polynomial time
options.explanation: No: it returns a solution within a chosen relative error ε of optimal, with running time growing polynomially in one over ε.

options.text: Vertex cover has a PTAS
options.explanation: Vertex cover is APX-hard (NP-hard to approximate below about 1.414), so it has no PTAS unless P equals NP.

That would contradict the stated hardness unless P equals NP.

lessons.title: Gap reductions and greedy set cover
lessons.summary: Large non-edge weights rule out constant-factor general-TSP approximation unless P equals NP.
lessons.body:
Approximation guarantees compare a feasible solution with the optimum on every permitted input. A hardness gap instead separates two kinds of input so widely that a good approximation would decide an NP-hard decision problem.

Fix any proposed approximation factor at least one. The general TSP trick reduces Hamiltonian cycle (is there a closed tour using only the graph's edges?) to TSP. Give each edge of an n-vertex graph weight 1 and each missing edge a huge weight w:

```formula essential
w = αn + 1
OPT_yes = n
c_no ≥ (n − 1) + w
c_no ≥ (1 + α)n > αn
where
w: the weight given to every pair of vertices that is not an edge of the graph
α: alpha, the approximation factor being ruled out, any constant at least 1
n: the number of vertices (cities)
OPT_yes: the length of the shortest tour when the graph has a Hamiltonian cycle: n edges of weight 1
c_no: the length of any tour when the graph has no Hamiltonian cycle, so the tour must use at least one missing edge
In words: with a Hamiltonian cycle the best tour costs n, so an α-approximation returns at most α × n. Without one, every tour costs more than α × n. Reading the approximation's output would decide an NP-complete problem.
```

This works only because non-metric weights can break the triangle inequality, which is why metric TSP escapes it.

For unweighted Set Cover, repeatedly choose the set covering most uncovered elements. Assume the available sets cover the whole universe. Its quality bound is a harmonic number, which grows logarithmically with the number of elements. The exact reference bound is:

```formula reference
H(n) = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … + 1/n
H(n) ≤ ln(n) + 1
where
H(n): the nth harmonic number: the sum of 1/1, 1/2, … up to 1/n
n: the number of elements to cover
ln(n): the natural logarithm of n (log to base e ≈ 2.718)
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the greedy cover uses at most a harmonic-number factor more sets than the optimum; this factor grows logarithmically with the universe size. Improving the leading logarithmic factor by any fixed positive fraction is NP-hard.
```

## Key takeaways

- Large non-edge weights rule out constant-factor general-TSP approximation unless P equals NP.
- The weighting trick relies on non-metric distances.
- Greedy set cover has a harmonic-number guarantee growing logarithmically.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [The Design of Approximation Algorithms — Williamson and Shmoys](https://www.designofapproxalgs.com/book.pdf)

lessons.title: PCP theorem gaps and the seven-eighths limit
lessons.summary: PCP theorem connects local random proof checks to hard approximation gaps.
lessons.body:
### Where the limits come from: the PCP theorem

The **PCP theorem** (Arora, Safra, Lund, Motwani, Sudan and Szegedy, 1992) says every NP statement has a polynomial-length proof format that a polynomial-time verifier, using logarithmically many random bits, can check by reading only a **constant number of randomly chosen bits**, catching any false claim with probability at least 1/2. An equivalent form is a gap that is hard to see:

```formula essential
f_max = 1   or   f_max ≤ s
where
f_max: the largest fraction of a 3-SAT formula's clauses that any true/false assignment satisfies, between 0 and 1
s: a fixed constant below 1 given by the theorem
In words: given a 3-SAT formula that is either fully satisfiable or can have at most a fraction s of its clauses satisfied, telling which is NP-hard. A deterministic algorithm guaranteeing a fraction of the optimum strictly greater than s would distinguish these promised cases, contradicting the gap hardness unless P equals NP. Randomised guarantees need a corresponding randomised-hardness assumption.
```

The sharpest result is Håstad's (2001), for MAX-3SAT with three distinct variables per clause. A clause (a ∨ b ∨ c) is "a OR b OR c", so it fails only when all three are false. A uniformly random assignment makes each clause false only when all three independent variable choices falsify their literals: one of eight equally likely settings. Each clause is therefore satisfied with probability seven eighths. Adding expectations gives seven eighths of all clauses on average, even if clauses share variables. Conditional expectation can turn this into a deterministic guarantee.

Håstad proved that guaranteeing any fixed positive improvement over seven eighths of the optimum is NP-hard. This is a worst-case guarantee over instances, not a claim that no particular formula can be solved exactly.

> [!warning] Proven versus conjectured hardness
> The vertex-cover limit of about 1.414 (the square root of 2) is a theorem conditional only on P differing from NP (Khot, Minzer and Safra, 2017–18; it improved Dinur and Safra's 1.36). The limit of 2 relies on the **Unique Games Conjecture** (Khot, 2002), which is open. Always check which assumption a hardness-of-approximation result uses.

These limits have different assumptions. A theorem conditional on the Unique Games Conjecture cannot be reported as following from P differing from NP alone.

Two other barriers need only P differing from NP: general, non-metric TSP has no constant-factor approximation, and Set Cover cannot beat its natural-logarithm-of-universe-size factor by any fixed proportional margin. The TSP barrier follows from a gap reduction from Hamiltonian Cycle; Dinur and Steurer established the Set Cover barrier in 2014.

## Key takeaways

- PCP theorem connects local random proof checks to hard approximation gaps.
- Independent fair variable choices satisfy seven eighths of distinct-variable clauses in expectation.
- Vertex-cover hardness near two uses UGC; hardness near the square root of two does not.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Optimal inapproximability — Håstad](https://people.kth.se/~johanh/optimalinap.pdf)
- [The 2-to-2 games result — Khot, Minzer and Safra](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2023/198-1/p01)
- [Set Cover hardness — Dinur and Steurer](https://www.dsteurer.org/paper/productgames.pdf)

lessons.title: Confine exponential search to a parameter
lessons.summary: FPT permits an arbitrary computable parameter factor with a fixed polynomial input exponent.
lessons.body:
## Option 4: parameterised algorithms

Sometimes the hardness lives in one small number. FPT means a computable parameter-only factor multiplied by a polynomial in total input length whose exponent is fixed independently of the parameter. A fixed parameter can make an exact algorithm useful, but neither factor is automatically small. A problem is **fixed-parameter tractable (FPT)** in parameter k if it can be solved in this much time:

```formula essential
T(n, k) = f(k) poly(n)
where
T(n, k): the running time, in basic steps
n: the input size, in bits
k: the parameter, a number you expect to be small, such as the solution size
f(k): any computable function of k alone, possibly exponential such as 2^k, but not involving n
poly(n): some polynomial in n, such as n^2 or n^3
In words: all the explosive growth is confined to the small parameter k; for a fixed k, the time grows only polynomially with the input, with an exponent that does not depend on k.
```

### Vertex cover by bounded branching

Any cover must contain u or v for an edge (u, v). Branch on both choices, with budget k − 1 each:

```python
def vc_fpt(edges, k):
    # returns a cover of size <= k, or None
    if not edges:
        return set()
    if k == 0:
        return None
    u, v = edges[0]
    for w in (u, v):
        # Choosing w covers all its incident
        # edges.
        rest = [e for e in edges
                if w not in e]
        sub = vc_fpt(rest, k - 1)
        if sub is not None:
            return sub | {w}
    return None

print(vc_fpt([(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)], 2))
# {1, 3}: also a minimum cover
print(vc_fpt([(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)], 1))
# None
```

The recursion tree has depth at most k and branching factor 2, so it has at most 2 to the power k leaves and fewer than twice as many nodes overall. Each nonterminal node filters an edge list of at most m edges for each of its two branches:

```formula reference
T = O(2^k m)
where
T: the running time, in basic steps
O(...): Big O: grows at most as fast as a constant times the expression inside
k: the nonnegative cover-size budget
m: the original number of edges; each branch filters its current edge list
2^k: 2 to the power k: the most leaves a binary recursion of depth k can have
In words: the search-tree factor depends exponentially on the cover budget, while each node filters edges. Fixing the budget keeps growth polynomial in the graph size; this bound counts list work, not wall-clock seconds.
```

Holding the cover budget fixed leaves only polynomial growth as the graph grows. Raising the budget increases the branching part rapidly. Compare this with enumerating every vertex subset of the requested size, where the exponent of graph size grows with that size. Both the budget and edge count matter in practice.

The code assumes a finite simple undirected graph and a nonnegative integer budget. It keeps Python edge lists in memory; the displayed bound counts list operations for a nonempty graph. An empty edge list returns immediately. The bound does not predict a measured runtime.

## Key takeaways

- FPT permits an arbitrary computable parameter factor with a fixed polynomial input exponent.
- Branching on an edge’s two endpoints gives a vertex-cover search tree of bounded depth.
- Operation-count estimates do not predict measured wall time.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

lessons.title: Problem kernels and limits of parameterisation
lessons.summary: High-degree vertices are forced into small vertex covers.
lessons.body:
### Kernelisation

A **problem kernel** is a polynomial-time shrinking step that leaves an equivalent instance whose size depends only on k. Buss's rule for vertex cover, where the degree of a vertex is its number of edges:

1. A vertex with degree greater than k **must** be in any cover of size at most k (otherwise all its more-than-k neighbours would be needed). Take it and decrease k. Repeat this rule until no such vertex remains, rejecting if the budget becomes negative.
2. Afterwards, every vertex has degree at most k, so k vertices cover at most k² edges. If more than k² edges remain, answer no.

Remove isolated vertices as well. What remains is small:

```formula reference
E_max = kk = k^2
V_max = 2k^2
where
E_max: the most edges the remaining instance can have if a cover of size k exists
V_max: the most vertices it can have, since each edge has two ends and no vertex is isolated
k: the remaining cover budget, after forced vertices have been taken
In words: after high-degree vertices are handled, the remaining budget times the maximum degree bounds how many edges any cover can touch. Reject larger instances; removing isolated vertices then bounds the remaining vertex count too. The kernel size depends only on the remaining budget.
```

Kernels are a standard preprocessing step in practical solvers.

### Not everything is FPT

Clique (a set of vertices all joined to each other) parameterised by solution size is **W[1]-hard**: no FPT algorithm is expected unless the parameterised classes FPT and W[1] coincide, and general algorithms still have an input-size exponent growing with the clique size, including speedups using fast matrix multiplication. The **Exponential Time Hypothesis** (ETH; Impagliazzo and Paturi, 2001) conjectures a positive exponential rate for 3-SAT in its number of variables, ruling out subexponential-time algorithms. Under ETH, Clique has no algorithm with a computable parameter-only factor and an input-size exponent growing sublinearly in the requested clique size.

ETH is a conjecture, stronger than P differs from NP.

## Key takeaways

- High-degree vertices are forced into small vertex covers.
- Buss’s rules give a problem kernel bounded in size by the remaining budget.
- Clique is W[1]-hard by solution size; ETH gives stronger conditional exponent limits.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

lessons.title: Choosing heuristics and measuring solvers
lessons.summary: Local search and metaheuristics trade universal quality promises for measured performance.
lessons.body:
## Option 5: heuristics and solvers

Heuristics generally give up a universal quality guarantee and must be measured on the intended workload:

- **Local search**: start somewhere, make small improving changes. 2-opt for TSP swaps two edges when that improves the tour. Its quality depends on the initial route and instance; it has no universal few-percent guarantee.
- **Metaheuristics**: simulated annealing, tabu search, genetic algorithms. Tunable, but the label alone gives no polynomial-time worst-case quality guarantee.
- **CDCL SAT solvers** (MiniSat, CaDiCaL, Kissat) and **MIP solvers** solve many large industrial instances for hardware verification, scheduling and planning; measure them on the intended workload.

## Choosing a strategy

1. Look for structure: is it bipartite, a tree, small treewidth, 2-SAT?
2. Is there a small parameter (budget, solution size)? Try FPT and problem kernels.
3. Need a guarantee on quality? Use an approximation algorithm, and check what the hardness results say is possible.
4. Need optimal answers on real data? Encode for a SAT/MIP solver and measure.
5. Need something good, fast? Heuristics, ideally seeded from an approximation.

For a delivery deadline, benchmark a construction such as nearest neighbour or a savings method, then improve it using 2-opt, Or-opt or guided local search. OR-Tools supplies routing machinery for such experiments. A valid relaxation can provide a lower bound: a route costing 1,050 kilometres against a positive lower bound of 1,000 kilometres is at most five percent above the optimum. The actual optimum may lie between the bound and the route cost. A solver’s reported gap depends on its convention, so state the denominator. No universal tour-quality or runtime percentage follows without a reproducible benchmark.

## Key takeaways

- Local search and metaheuristics trade universal quality promises for measured performance.
- Exact SAT and MIP solvers remain useful on structured inputs.
- Choose a strategy from structure, parameters, quality requirements and deadlines.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

lessons.title: Measuring working memory
lessons.summary: Read-only input is excluded from the working-space count.
lessons.body:
Time is not the only resource. A route planner on an embedded device, a streaming algorithm watching a network link, or a game engine searching ahead are all limited by **memory**. Space complexity asks how much working memory a problem needs.

Space behaves differently from time for one reason: **space can be reused, time cannot.** That single fact drives every result in this lesson.

## Measuring space

We use a Turing machine with a **read-only input tape** and a separate **work tape**, and count only the work-tape cells used. That makes sublinear space meaningful: a machine can read an n-bit input while storing only a few counters.

- **SPACE(s(n))**: problems decidable by a deterministic machine using O(s(n)) work cells.
- **NSPACE(s(n))**: the same with a nondeterministic machine.

The key classes are defined by plugging particular space bounds into these:

```formula reference
L = SPACE(log n)
NL = NSPACE(log n)
PSPACE = SPACE(n^k)   for some k
EXPSPACE = SPACE(2^{n^k})   for some k
where
SPACE(s(n)): the problems a deterministic machine (no guessing) decides using at most a constant times s(n) cells of work tape
NSPACE(s(n)): the same, for a nondeterministic machine (one that may guess at each step)
s(n): the space bound: a function of the input size n, counted in work-tape cells
n: the input size, in bits
log: the logarithm, base 2; encoding a position among n positions takes about this many bits, with integer rounding
k: a fixed constant exponent, such as 1, 2 or 3
L: logarithmic space, deterministic
NL: nondeterministic logarithmic space
PSPACE: polynomial space: a problem is in PSPACE when it is in SPACE(n^k) for some fixed k
EXPSPACE: exponential space: SPACE(2 to the power n^k) for some fixed k
In words: L and NL allow only logarithmic work memory (without and with guessing); PSPACE allows memory polynomial in the input size; EXPSPACE allows exponential memory. Their definitions constrain working space rather than imposing an explicit time bound. Deciders must still halt, and configuration counting gives an implicit deterministic time bound.
```

| Class | Space bound | Example |
|---|---|---|
| L | logarithmic | Undirected reachability |
| NL | logarithmic, guessing | Directed reachability |
| PSPACE | polynomial | TQBF, generalised games |
| EXPSPACE | exponential | Regex equivalence with squaring |

Why logarithmic? It is just enough to hold a constant number of pointers into the input, or counters up to the input size. Think of a log-space algorithm as keeping a fixed number of input positions and small counters while rereading the input as needed. Doubling the input length adds only about one bit per position counter.

## Key takeaways

- Read-only input is excluded from the working-space count.
- Logarithmic work memory can store a fixed number of input positions.
- Space classes distinguish deterministic from nondeterministic computation.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

lessons.title: How space bounds time
lessons.summary: Time bounds space because each step touches limited memory.
lessons.body:
## Time versus space

Two simple facts relate the resources:

1. **Time bounds space.** In t steps a machine can touch at most t cells.
2. **Space bounds time, exponentially.** A machine with a small work tape has only a limited number of distinct **machine configurations** (head positions, tape contents, state). A halting deterministic computation never repeats a configuration, so it finishes within that many steps.

```formula essential
TIME(t) ⊆ SPACE(t)
SPACE(s) ⊆ TIME(2^{O(s)})   for s ≥ log n
where
TIME(t): the problems a deterministic machine decides in at most a constant times t steps
SPACE(s): the problems a deterministic machine decides using at most a constant times s work-tape cells
t: a time bound, in steps
s: a space bound, in work-tape cells
n: the input size, in bits
log: logarithm base 2
O(s): Big O: at most a constant times s, for large inputs
2^{O(s)}: 2 raised to a power that is at most a constant times s
⊆: "is contained in": every problem in the left class is also in the right class
≥: is at least
In words: a time bound also bounds the work cells a machine can visit. A halting deterministic computation with at least logarithmic workspace takes at most exponentially many steps in that space bound, up to constants in the exponent.
```

The second fact comes from counting configurations:

```formula reference
N_conf ≤ (n + 2)s|Γ|^s|Q|
N_conf = 2^{O(s)}   for s ≥ log n
where
N_conf: the number of distinct configurations the machine can be in
n: the input size; the read-only input has n symbols plus two end-marker positions
s: the positive number of available work-tape cells, also bounding work-head positions
Γ: gamma, the fixed work-tape alphabet; |Γ| is its number of symbols
|Γ|^s: the number of possible work-tape contents: |Γ| choices for each of s cells
Q: the fixed set of control states; |Q| is its size
log: logarithm base 2; s ≥ log n means the tape has at least enough cells to hold one pointer into the input
O(s): Big O: at most a constant times s
≤: is at most
In words: multiply the choices for both head positions, work-tape contents and control state. For a fixed machine with at least logarithmic workspace, the result is at most exponential in that workspace bound.
```

With these, logarithmic space fits in polynomial time and polynomial space fits in exponential time. Directed reachability also puts NL inside P; deterministic polynomial time is inside NP, and NP is inside PSPACE. These containments do not establish which neighbouring classes differ.

NP sits inside PSPACE because a polynomial-space machine can try every certificate one after another, **reusing** the same space for each.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Reusing a whiteboard
> Work through a stack of tasks on one whiteboard, erasing each task before beginning the next.
>
> **How it maps:** Certificate enumeration reuses the same workspace for each check. More checks increase total time, while only one check's storage is needed at once.
>
> **Where it stops:** The machine must also store its current certificate and enumeration counter. Reuse saves simultaneous storage; it does not make the exponentially many checks fast.

## Key takeaways

- Time bounds space because each step touches limited memory.
- A halting deterministic computation cannot repeat a configuration.
- Counting configurations gives exponential-time simulations of bounded space.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

lessons.title: Directed reachability and logarithmic space
lessons.summary: A nondeterministic machine guesses a path using a vertex and a counter.
lessons.body:
## Directed reachability and NL

**PATH**: given a directed graph and vertices s, t, is there a path from s to t?

A nondeterministic log-space machine guesses the path one vertex at a time, storing only the current vertex and a step counter, and gives up after n steps (n being the number of vertices). If a path exists, removing cycles gives one shorter than the vertex count. Vertex names and the counter need only logarithmically many bits; the machine checks each proposed edge by reading the input.

So PATH is in NL. It is also **NL-complete** under log-space reductions.

For **undirected** graphs, Reingold (2005) proved reachability is in deterministic L, a celebrated and difficult result. Whether L equals NL (equivalently, whether directed PATH is in L) is open.

## Key takeaways

- A nondeterministic machine guesses a path using a vertex and a counter.
- Directed reachability is NL-complete under log-space reductions.
- Undirected reachability is in deterministic L; L versus NL remains open.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

lessons.title: Savitch’s midpoint recursion
lessons.summary: Try each candidate midpoint and recurse on two shorter path bounds.
lessons.body:
## Savitch's theorem

Does nondeterminism help for space as much as it seems to for time? Much less, it turns out.

**Savitch's theorem (1970)** applies to space-constructible bounds at least logarithmic in input length. Space-constructible means the machine can mark out the permitted workspace within that bound. The standard bounds used here meet this condition.

```formula essential
NSPACE(s) ⊆ SPACE(s^2)   for s ≥ log n
where
NSPACE(s): problems a nondeterministic (guessing) machine decides using at most a constant times s work-tape cells
SPACE(s^2): problems a deterministic machine decides using at most a constant times s squared cells
s: a space-constructible space bound, in cells; the machine can mark off that many cells within that order of space
n: the input size, in bits
log: logarithm base 2
⊆: "is contained in"
≥: is at least
In words: a deterministic simulation needs at most quadratic growth in the original space bound. This is an asymptotic guarantee with hidden constants, not an exact allocation of memory cells.
```

The idea is a midpoint recursion:

```formula essential
R(u, v, t)  iff  ∃ w with
  R(u, w, ⌈t/2⌉) and R(w, v, ⌊t/2⌋)
where
R(u, v, t): "there is a path from vertex u to vertex v of length at most t edges"
u, v: the start and end vertices
w: a candidate midpoint vertex
t: an integer maximum path length of at least two, in edges
⌈ ⌉, ⌊ ⌋: ceiling rounds up and floor rounds down; the two integer half-bounds sum to t
∃: "there exists": at least one such w
In words: a path of at most t edges exists exactly when some middle vertex splits it into two parts bounded by the rounded-up and rounded-down halves. If the path is shorter than the bound, choose the midpoint along that shorter path; allowing a zero-length part handles an endpoint.
```

Try every w, recursing on both halves, and **reuse** the space between the two calls.

```python
def reach(adj, u, v, t):
    # is there a path u -> v of length <= t?
    # (called with t >= 1)
    if t <= 1:
        return u == v or v in adj[u]
    # Integer halves add up to the full
    # bound.
    h = (t + 1) // 2
    return any(reach(adj, u, w, h) and
               reach(adj, w, v, t - h)
               for w in adj)

adj = {0: [1], 1: [2], 2: [3],
       3: [], 4: [0]}
n = len(adj)
print(reach(adj, 0, 3, n))   # True
print(reach(adj, 3, 0, n))   # False
print(reach(adj, 4, 3, n))   # True: via 0
print(reach(adj, 0, 3, 2))   # False: 3 hops
```

The adjacency dictionary must include every vertex, including sinks. The initial bound is a positive integer. The function reads an explicit graph already held by the caller; the space theorem concerns additional workspace, not the memory needed to store that input dictionary. Python frame and integer overhead are larger than the bit-packed model.

## Key takeaways

- Try each candidate midpoint and recurse on two shorter path bounds.
- Sequential recursive invocations reuse workspace.
- The Python example demonstrates the recursion on an explicit graph.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

lessons.title: Squaring space to remove nondeterminism
lessons.summary: Logarithmic recursion depth times logarithmic frame size gives squared-logarithmic space.
lessons.body:
Continue the length-bounded reachability recursion: try a midpoint, check both halves in sequence, and retain only the current stack. The graph is read-only input; the analysis below counts additional abstract workspace rather than Python object sizes.

Space analysis for a graph with n vertices:

- Recursion depth: the length bound halves each level, so there are about log₂ n levels.
- Each stack frame holds four numbers (u, v, w and the length), each at most n, so a frame is a logarithmic number of bits.
- Multiply them for the total.

```formula essential
d = ⌈log_2(n)⌉
S = d O(log n) = O(log^2 n)
where
d: the number of halvings before the base case; including its frame adds one
S: the total work memory, in bits
n: the number of vertices
log_2: logarithm base 2
log^2 n: (log n) squared
⌈ ⌉: ceiling, rounding up to a whole number
O(...): Big O: at most a constant times this, for large n
≈: approximately equal to
bits: binary digits
In words: logarithmically many live recursion frames, each holding logarithmically many bits, give squared-logarithmic working space. The full search tree is never stored.
```

The price is time. Each level tries every midpoint and makes two calls, so the number of branches multiplies at every level:

```formula reference
T = O((2n)^{⌈log_2(n)⌉})
T = n^{O(log n)}
where
T: an upper-bound analysis of recursive-call work
⌈ ⌉: ceiling, rounding up to a whole number
O(...): Big O, an upper bound up to fixed factors for sufficiently large n
n: the number of vertices
log_2: logarithm base 2
O(log n): Big O: at most a constant times log n
≤: is at most
≈: approximately equal to
In words: trying every midpoint at each recursive level yields a quasi-polynomial time upper bound. This space-saving simulation does not establish a polynomial-time bound; particular graphs can terminate much sooner.
```

Savitch trades time for space. The midpoint equivalence proves the general reachability statement; keeping only the current recursion stack gives the space saving.

For a nondeterministic machine using space s, apply the same recursion to its **configuration graph** (one vertex per configuration, an edge for each legal step):

```formula essential
N = 2^{O(s)}
d = log_2(N) = O(s)
S = d O(s) = O(s^2)
where
N: the number of vertices (configurations) of the configuration graph
s: the machine's space bound, in cells
d: the recursion depth
S: the total work memory of the deterministic simulation
log_2: logarithm base 2
O(s): Big O: at most a constant times s
In words: there are about 2 to the power s configurations, so the recursion is about s levels deep, each frame storing a few configurations of about s cells: s squared space in total.
```

> [!note] Consequence: PSPACE equals NPSPACE
> The square of a polynomial is a polynomial, so nondeterminism adds nothing to polynomial space. Compare time, where P vs NP is open.

## Key takeaways

- Logarithmic recursion depth times logarithmic frame size gives squared-logarithmic space.
- Time can be quasi-polynomial while work memory stays tiny.
- Applying the recursion to configurations proves PSPACE equals NPSPACE.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

lessons.title: Why NL equals coNL
lessons.summary: Immerman–Szelepcsényi closes nondeterministic space under complement.
lessons.body:
NL is nondeterministic logarithmic working space, with input kept separately read-only. Directed reachability is NL-complete. Here the complement asks for a certificate that the destination is unreachable; this is distinct from finding a path.

## NL equals coNL

**Immerman–Szelepcsényi theorem (proved independently, 1987–88)** applies to the standard space-constructible bounds at least logarithmic in input length used here:

```formula essential
NSPACE(s) = coNSPACE(s)   for s ≥ log n
NL = coNL
where
NSPACE(s): problems a nondeterministic machine decides using at most a constant times s work cells
coNSPACE(s): the complements of those problems (yes and no swapped)
NL: nondeterministic logarithmic space
coNL: the complements of NL problems
s: a space-constructible space bound, in cells
n: the input size, in bits
log: logarithm base 2
≥: is at least
In words: for nondeterministic space of at least log n, a class equals its complement class. In particular **NL equals coNL**: a nondeterministic log-space machine can certify that t is *unreachable* from s.
```

The proof is "inductive counting": nondeterministically compute the exact number of vertices reachable within 1 step, then within 2 steps, and so on up to n steps, using each count to verify the next. Knowing exactly how many vertices are reachable lets the machine confirm t isn't among them.

The analogous question for time, NP vs coNP, is open and believed to go the other way.

At linear rather than logarithmic space, the same complement theorem applies to context-sensitive languages, recognised by linear-bounded nondeterministic machines. For 2-SAT unsatisfiability, guess a variable and directed implication paths both from it to its negation and back; this uses nondeterministic logarithmic space. Complement closure then puts 2-SAT satisfiability in NL too.

## Key takeaways

- Immerman–Szelepcsényi closes nondeterministic space under complement.
- Inductive counting certifies directed unreachability in NL.
- The result covers linear space too and says nothing comparable about NP versus coNP.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

lessons.title: Evaluating quantified Boolean formulas
lessons.summary: Quantifier order allows or forbids choices that depend on earlier variables.
lessons.body:
## PSPACE-completeness: TQBF

A **quantified Boolean formula** puts quantifiers in front of a formula:

```formula essential
∀x ∃y ∀z ((x ∨ y) ∧ (¬y ∨ z))
where
x, y, z: Boolean variables, each true or false
∀: "for all": the rest must hold for both values of the variable
∃: "there exists": the rest must hold for at least one value of the variable
∨: OR: true when at least one side is true
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
¬: NOT: ¬y is true exactly when y is false
In words: "for every x there is a y such that, for every z, (x or y) and (not y or z) both hold". This particular formula is false, as traced below.
```

**TQBF** asks whether a fully quantified formula is true. It is **PSPACE-complete** (Stockmeyer and Meyer, 1973). SAT is the special case where every quantifier is ∃.

A recursive evaluator uses polynomial space and has an exponential-time upper bound. Existential choices need one successful branch; universal choices need every branch to succeed:

```python
def tqbf(quants, phi, a=()):
    # quants: string of 'E'/'A', one per var
    if len(a) == len(quants):
        return phi(a)
    q = quants[len(a)]
    # Finish one branch before using the
    # next.
    r = tqbf(quants, phi, a + (False,))
    if q == 'E' and r:
        return True
    if q == 'A' and not r:
        return False
    return tqbf(quants, phi, a + (True,))

f = lambda a: a[0] != a[1]
print(tqbf('AE', f))  # True:  ∀x ∃y x≠y
print(tqbf('EA', f))  # False: ∃x ∀y x≠y

g = lambda a: ((a[0] or a[1]) and
               (not a[1] or a[2]))
print(tqbf('AEA', g))  # False
```

The recursion depth is the number of variables. A careful implementation keeps one shared assignment array and a constant amount of data per frame:

```formula reference
S = O(n + |φ|)
T = O(2^n × |φ|)
where
S: the working space: a shared n-bit assignment and quantifier stack, plus linear-in-formula workspace for evaluating φ
T: the running time, in steps
n: the number of variables (and so the recursion depth)
φ: phi, the quantifier-free part of the formula; |φ| is its length, the cost of evaluating it once
O(...): Big O: at most a constant times this
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a shared-assignment evaluator stores only the current assignment, stack and formula. It may explore exponentially many assignments in sequence, so polynomial space does not imply polynomial time.
```

(This Python version copies the tuple at each level, which costs space quadratic in n: still polynomial.)

Trace the last one: if x is false, (x ∨ y) forces y true, and then (¬y ∨ z) requires z true for **all** z, which fails when z is false. So the ∀x fails.

## Key takeaways

- Quantifier order allows or forbids choices that depend on earlier variables.
- Depth-first evaluation reuses memory across truth assignments.
- TQBF is PSPACE-complete, with SAT as the all-existential case.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

# Compare dependent and fixed choices.

lessons.title: Sharing the reachability formula
lessons.summary: A naive reachability formula doubles its subformula at every level.
lessons.body:
TQBF asks whether a fully quantified Boolean formula is true and can be evaluated in polynomial space. To establish completeness we also need PSPACE-hardness: turn any polynomial-space computation into a polynomial-size quantified formula.

Hardness, in outline: for a machine using space p(n), write a formula saying "configuration c1 reaches configuration c2 within 2 to the power k steps", defined recursively using a midpoint:

```formula essential
R(c1, c2, k) = ∃m ∀c3 ∀c4
  [((c3, c4) = (c1, m) ∨
    (c3, c4) = (m, c2))
   → R(c3, c4, k − 1)]
|R(k)| = |R(k − 1)| + O(p(n))
|R(k)| = O(kp(n)) = O(p(n)^2)
where
R(c1, c2, k): the formula "configuration c1 reaches configuration c2 in at most 2^k steps"
c1, c2: the start and end configurations, each written as about p(n) Boolean variables
m: the midpoint configuration
c3, c4: universally quantified configuration encodings; the implication constrains the recursive check only when this pair equals one of the two halves
n: the input length in bits
[ ]: grouping the implication; vector equality means equality of every corresponding bit
k: the recursion level; k = O(p(n)), because the machine has at most 2^{O(p(n))} configurations
p(n): the machine's polynomial space bound on an n-bit input
|R(k)|: the length of the formula at level k
∃: "there exists"; ∀: "for all"
∨: OR; →: implies ("if the left side holds, the right side must too")
O(...): Big O: at most a constant times this
In words: one copy of the level-(k − 1) formula serves both halves, because ∀ makes it check whichever pair is plugged in. Each level adds only about p(n) symbols, so the whole formula is polynomial size.
```

The midpoint is chosen first, and universal variables then require both endpoint pairs to pass the one shared recursive test. Other pairs make the implication automatically true.

The naive version would write the sub-formula twice per level and double in size each time, giving exponentially many copies. This is Savitch's recursion written as a formula.

The base case says that the configurations are equal or joined by one legal machine step. Each configuration is a polynomial-length Boolean vector, and each quantified vector abbreviates one quantifier for each of its bits. Fresh bound-variable names avoid capture when a recursive template is substituted. One may arrange a unique accepting configuration without changing the polynomial-space bound.

## Key takeaways

- A naive reachability formula doubles its subformula at every level.
- Universal configuration variables let one copy check both halves.
- Polynomial formula length establishes PSPACE-hardness.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

  ∧ R(m, c2, k − 1)]
where
