lessons.title: Games, regexes and proven space separations
lessons.summary: Polynomial-length games can be evaluated in polynomial space.
lessons.body:
## Games are PSPACE problems

Alternating quantifiers are a two-player game: "there is a move for me such that for all your replies there is a move for me such that...". TQBF is a game in which players take turns setting variables.

With polynomial-size positions and polynomial-space move generation and end-of-play evaluation, polynomially bounded play gives PSPACE membership by depth-first search. Hardness requires a separate reduction; the following generalised game families are **PSPACE-complete**:

- **Generalised geography** (players extend a path in a directed graph, no repeats), PSPACE-complete.
- **Generalised Hex** and generalised **Othello** on n × n boards, PSPACE-complete.

Games that can last exponentially long are typically harder: generalised **chess** (Fraenkel and Lichtenstein, 1981) and **generalised Go** with the simple-ko rule variant analysed by Robson (Robson, 1983) on n × n boards are **EXPTIME-complete**, so provably not in P.

Real-world PSPACE-complete problems include **equivalence of ordinary regular expressions** using union, concatenation and Kleene star (excluding backreferences and succinct extensions), **LTL model checking** used in hardware and protocol verification, and finite propositional **AI planning** (ground STRIPS plan existence).

## What's proven, what's open

For space-constructible bounds at least logarithmic in input length, the **space hierarchy theorem** says asymptotically more space solves strictly more problems. Space-constructibility means the machine can mark out its workspace within the stated bound; standard linear and polynomial bounds satisfy it:

```formula essential
SPACE(s) ⊊ SPACE(s′)   when s = o(s′)
SPACE(n) ⊊ SPACE(n^2)
where
SPACE(s): problems a deterministic machine decides using at most a constant times s work cells
s, s′: two space bounds (s′ is read "s prime"); s′ must be space-constructible and at least log n (the machine can mark off the bound within that amount of space)
n: the input size, in bits
o(s′): little o: grows strictly more slowly than s′, so s / s′ shrinks towards 0 as n grows
⊊: "is strictly contained in": every problem on the left is on the right, and some problem on the right is not on the left
In words: give a machine asymptotically more memory and it can decide problems it could not before. For example, quadratic space decides strictly more than linear space.
```

Combined with Savitch's theorem, this proves some separations:

```formula essential
NL ⊆ SPACE(log^2 n) ⊊ PSPACE
PSPACE ⊊ EXPSPACE
P ⊊ EXPTIME
where
NL: nondeterministic logarithmic space
SPACE(log^2 n): deterministic space of at most a constant times (log n) squared
PSPACE: polynomial space
EXPSPACE: exponential space
P: polynomial time
EXPTIME: exponential time
n: the input size, in bits
log: logarithm base 2
⊆: "is contained in"
⊊: "is strictly contained in": contained, and not equal
In words: NL is strictly smaller than PSPACE, PSPACE strictly smaller than EXPSPACE, and P strictly smaller than EXPTIME (the last from the time hierarchy theorem).
```

- **Proven**: the three strict separations above.
- **Open**: L vs NL, L vs P, NL vs P, P vs PSPACE, NP vs PSPACE, PSPACE vs EXPTIME.

It is striking that P equalling PSPACE has not been ruled out: nobody can prove that polynomial memory gives more power than polynomial time, though it is universally conjectured.

For ordinary regex equivalence, first build linear-size NFAs and consider pairs of subset states. A distinguishing string exists exactly when a reachable pair has different acceptance answers. Although the implicit product graph may have exponentially many vertices, each vertex and a path-length counter need only polynomially many bits. Nondeterministic reachability uses polynomial space, and Savitch removes nondeterminism. Building and remembering every visited DFA state may instead consume exponential memory. Backreferences and succinct repetition operators require separate complexity analyses.

## Key takeaways

- Polynomial-length games can be evaluated in polynomial space.
- Completeness depends on the game rules and generalised input family.
- NL differs from PSPACE and PSPACE differs from EXPSPACE; P versus PSPACE is open.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)

lessons.title: Las Vegas, Monte Carlo and decision classes
lessons.summary: Las Vegas guarantees correctness; Monte Carlo permits bounded error.
lessons.body:
Some of the most useful algorithms flip coins. Miller–Rabin is widely used in probable-prime generation, randomised quicksort illustrates efficient expected-time sorting, and suitable secret keyed hashing can defend against precomputed adversarial collisions; a seed alone does not guarantee resistance to adaptive attacks. Randomness also gives us algorithms for problems where no deterministic polynomial algorithm is known at all.

Quantum computers go further: they manipulate amplitudes that can interfere. The later quantum lessons compare those capabilities with the randomised classes introduced here.

## Two kinds of randomised algorithm

- **Las Vegas**: always correct, running time is random. Randomised quicksort with distinct keys and uniform random pivots: always sorts, in an expected O(n log n) comparisons, where n is the number of keys.
- **Monte Carlo**: a bounded running-time guarantee, but some chance of a wrong answer. Actual running time can still vary. Miller–Rabin: may call a composite "probably prime".

The error probability is over the algorithm's own coin flips, for **every** input. No assumption about the input being random is needed.

## The classes

RP, coRP and BPP use a worst-case polynomial time bound; ZPP uses expected polynomial time.

| Class | If answer is yes | If answer is no |
|---|---|---|
| RP | accept with probability at least one half | always reject |
| coRP | always accept | reject with probability at least one half |
| BPP | accept with probability at least two thirds | reject with probability at least two thirds |
| ZPP | never wrong | expected poly time |

For RP, acceptance is conclusive; rejection may be a missed yes-instance. For coRP, rejection is conclusive; acceptance may be a missed no-instance. BPP has neither conclusive answer on a single run.

coRP swaps the roles (never wrongly rejects a yes-instance; rejects each no-instance with probability at least 1/2). ZPP sits exactly where the one-sided classes overlap:

```formula essential
ZPP = RP ∩ coRP
where
ZPP: zero-error probabilistic polynomial time: decision problems a randomised algorithm always answers correctly, in expected polynomial time
RP: randomised polynomial time: polynomial-time randomised algorithms that never accept a no-instance and accept each yes-instance with probability at least 1/2
coRP: the complements of RP problems: never reject a yes-instance, and reject each no-instance with probability at least 1/2
∩: intersection: the problems that belong to both classes
In words: a problem has a zero-error, expected-polynomial-time algorithm exactly when it has both kinds of one-sided-error algorithm. Run both repeatedly until one of them gives an answer that is certain.
```

The constants 1/2 and 2/3 don't matter, thanks to amplification.

## Key takeaways

- Las Vegas guarantees correctness; Monte Carlo permits bounded error.
- RP and coRP put errors on opposite input types.
- Combining both one-sided algorithms yields zero-error expected polynomial time.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Randomised complexity — Arora lecture notes](https://users.cs.duke.edu/~reif/courses/complectures/Arora/lec6.pdf)

lessons.title: Amplifying one-sided and two-sided decisions
lessons.summary: RP uses any-accept; coRP uses all-accept on independent trials.
lessons.body:
## Amplification

**One-sided error (RP).** Run the algorithm several times and accept if any run accepts. A no-instance is never accepted; a yes-instance is missed only if every run misses:

```formula reference
ε_k ≤ (1/2)^k = 2^{−k}
where
ε_k: the probability that all k independent runs miss a yes-instance
k: the positive number of independent runs
(1/2)^k: k copies of one-half multiplied together: each run misses with probability at most 1/2, and independent probabilities multiply
≤: is at most
≈: approximately equal to
In words: each fresh independent trial reduces the chance of missing a yes-instance by at least another factor of two. No-instance rejection remains certain.
```

**One-sided error (coRP).** Accept only if all independent trials accept; reject if any rejects. A yes-instance always passes, while a no-instance fools the combined test only when every trial falsely accepts. Miller–Rabin has this direction: declaring prime requires all bases to pass. Repeating an identical random base does not supply independent evidence.

**Two-sided error (BPP).** Run the algorithm an odd number of times and take the **majority vote** answer. The majority is wrong only when at least half of the runs are wrong:

```formula reference
ε_r = Σ C(r, i)p^i (1 − p)^{r−i}
  for (r + 1)/2 ≤ i ≤ r
ε_r ≤ e^{−cr}
where
ε_r: the probability that the majority of r independent runs is wrong
r: the positive odd number of independent runs
i: the number of runs that are wrong; the sum covers every i from (r + 1)/2 up to r
Σ: sum: add up the term after it for every value of i in the stated range
C(r, i): "r choose i", the number of ways to pick which i of the r runs are wrong
p: the error probability of one run; here 1/3
e: Euler's number, about 2.718, the base of natural exponentials
c: a positive constant depending on the fixed error p, which is strictly below one half; here p is one third (Chernoff gives an exponentially shrinking bound)
≈: approximately equal to
≤: is at most
In words: count every outcome with a wrong majority, including cases where only some trials fail. Independent repetitions with a fixed success advantage above one half reduce the majority error exponentially.
```

With three trials, the majority is wrong when either two or all three answers are wrong. Multiplying the probabilities of three wrong answers alone misses the first case. Reusing one random seed to repeat the identical computation provides no independent evidence.

So BPP with error 2 to the power −100 is the same class as BPP with error 1/3. The mathematical error bound assumes independent random choices and correct execution; it is not a hardware-reliability estimate.

Use positive odd trial counts to avoid ties and fresh independent randomness on each run, with a fixed per-run error strictly below one half. Without a success gap above one half, majority voting has no uniform polynomial-repetition guarantee.

## Key takeaways

- RP uses any-accept; coRP uses all-accept on independent trials.
- BPP uses majority voting with a success probability bounded above one half.
- The mathematical error bound assumes independent trials and correct execution.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Randomised complexity — Arora lecture notes](https://users.cs.duke.edu/~reif/courses/complectures/Arora/lec6.pdf)

lessons.title: Checking a matrix product with randomness
lessons.summary: Freivalds compares three matrix–vector products using exact arithmetic.
lessons.body:
## Randomness in action

### Freivalds: checking a matrix product

Multiplying two n × n matrices naively costs about n³ multiplications; subcubic algorithms also exist. The comparison below is with naive multiplication, not a claim about the current best exponent. Checking a claimed product is cheaper: using exact integer arithmetic or arithmetic in a field, pick a random vector of 0s and 1s and multiply it through both sides.

```formula essential
A × (B × r) = C × r
where
A, B: the two n × n input matrices
C: the claimed product of A and B, an n × n matrix
r: a random column vector of n independently sampled entries, each uniformly 0 or 1
B × r: a matrix–vector product: n^2 multiplications, giving a vector of n numbers
n: the number of rows and columns of each square matrix
In words: multiply the random vector by the second matrix, then the first, and compare with multiplying it by the claimed product. Correct products agree for every vector; each trial needs only three matrix–vector products.
```

Each trial uses quadratically many arithmetic operations in the matrix side length, instead of the cubic work of naive full multiplication.

If C is wrong, a single trial exposes it with probability at least 1/2, so the chance that t independent trials all miss is at most 2 to the power −t (about one in a million for t = 20).

```python
import random

def freivalds(A, B, C, trials=20):
    n = len(A)
    def mul(M, x):
        return [sum(M[i][j] * x[j]
                    for j in range(n))
                for i in range(n)]
    # All trials must pass to accept the
    # product.
    for _ in range(trials):
        r = [random.randint(0, 1)
             for _ in range(n)]
        if mul(A, mul(B, r)) != mul(C, r):
            return False  # surely wrong
    return True  # wrong w.p. <= 2**-trials

A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
B = [[5, 6], [7, 8]]
good = [[19, 22], [43, 50]]
bad = [[19, 22], [43, 51]]
print(freivalds(A, B, good))  # True
print(freivalds(A, B, bad))
# Usually False; True with chance 2**-20.
```

For `bad`, the only wrong entry is at row 1, column 1 (0-indexed), so a trial catches it exactly when the random vector's entry `r[1]` is 1, with probability exactly 1/2.

For any incorrect product, choose a nonzero row of the difference from the true product and a nonzero coefficient in that row. Hold all other random-vector entries fixed. At most one of the two choices for this coefficient’s entry can make the row’s dot product zero. Thus at least half the vectors detect an error, without needing an empirical benchmark.

These are arithmetic-operation counts, not a claim that unbounded integer multiplication costs one bit operation. Intermediate integer lengths and input encoding matter for bit complexity. Floating-point rounding can also invalidate the exact one-sided guarantee. Python’s random module illustrates ideal independent draws in the mathematical model; a finite pseudorandom generator is not itself a proof of independent randomness.

## Key takeaways

- Freivalds compares three matrix–vector products using exact arithmetic.
- Correct products always pass; incorrect products pass a trial with probability at most one half.
- Independent trials that all accept multiply false-positive bounds.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Randomised complexity — Arora lecture notes](https://users.cs.duke.edu/~reif/courses/complectures/Arora/lec6.pdf)

options.text: The product is wrong with probability only one half
options.explanation: One half bounds the chance a wrong product escapes one trial, not the certainty of a detected mismatch.

options.explanation: Three matrix–vector products suffice to exhibit a mismatch.

options.text: Floating-point implementations have the same exact guarantee automatically

A mismatch is conclusive; repeated agreement is only bounded-error evidence.

lessons.title: Polynomial identities and probable primes
lessons.summary: Schwartz–Zippel bounds false zeros using degree and sample-set size.
lessons.body:
### Polynomial identity testing

Given an arithmetic circuit over a specified field (a network of additions and multiplications) computing a polynomial in many variables, is that polynomial identically zero, meaning every coefficient cancels? Expanding it can produce exponentially many terms.

The **Schwartz–Zippel lemma** says a random evaluation almost never lands on a root of a nonzero polynomial:

```formula reference
Pr[p(x_1, ..., x_n) = 0] ≤ d / |S|
where
p: the polynomial computed by the circuit, assumed not to be the zero polynomial
x_1, ..., x_n: its n variables, each chosen independently and uniformly at random from S
n: the number of variables
d: an upper bound on the total degree of p, the largest sum of exponents in any term
S: a finite nonempty set of distinct values from the coefficient field
|S|: the number of values in S
Pr[...]: the probability, over the random choice of the variables, of the event in brackets
≤: is at most
In words: for a nonzero polynomial, the false-zero bound is total degree divided by sample-set size. A larger sample set improves the bound; more variables alone do not worsen it.
```

So evaluate at one random point: if the result is nonzero, the polynomial is certainly nonzero. Repeating with independent points multiplies the bounds. Choose each variable independently and uniformly from the same finite set of distinct elements in the coefficient field (or integral domain). A known total-degree upper bound divided by the sample-set size bounds a false zero. The bound is useful when the sample set is larger than that degree bound. Every evaluation of an identically zero polynomial is zero.

For the standard arithmetic-circuit identity-testing problem, with an effective coefficient representation, a computable degree bound and polynomial-cost exact or suitable modular evaluations, polynomial identity testing is in **coRP**, and **no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is known**. Kabanets and Impagliazzo (2004) showed that derandomising it would imply circuit lower bounds that nobody can currently prove.

### Primality: a derandomisation story

Miller–Rabin declares a composite "probably prime" with probability at most 1/4 per random base, and independent bases multiply:

```formula reference
ε_k ≤ (1/4)^k = 2^{−2 × k}
where
ε_k: the probability that a fixed odd composite passes all k independent rounds
k: the positive number of rounds, each with a fresh uniformly sampled permitted base
(1/4)^k: k copies of one-quarter multiplied together
≤: is at most
≈: approximately equal to
In words: each independent uniformly sampled permitted base reduces a fixed odd composite’s chance of passing all tests by at least another factor of four. A prime is never rejected.
```

This put PRIMES in coRP (composites are detected with one-sided error) decades ago. In 2002 the AKS algorithm put PRIMES in **P**. Practical libraries still use Miller–Rabin because it is efficient; actual performance depends on operand sizes and implementation. The one-quarter bound is for each fixed odd composite with independent uniformly chosen permitted bases, not the posterior probability that a generated candidate is composite after passing.

## Key takeaways

- Schwartz–Zippel bounds false zeros using degree and sample-set size.
- Primality testing illustrates coRP amplification by accepting only when all rounds pass.
- AKS proves primality belongs to deterministic polynomial time.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Randomised complexity — Arora lecture notes](https://users.cs.duke.edu/~reif/courses/complectures/Arora/lec6.pdf)
- [PRIMES is in P — original paper](https://cse.iitk.ac.in/users/manindra/algebra/primality_original.pdf)

lessons.title: What is proven about BPP
lessons.summary: RP is in NP because an accepting random string is a certificate.
lessons.body:
## How BPP relates to the rest

The proven containments:

```formula essential
P ⊆ ZPP ⊆ RP ⊆ BPP
RP ⊆ NP
BPP ⊆ PSPACE
BPP ⊆ Σ₂ ∩ Π₂
BPP ⊆ P/poly
where
P: the complexity class P: decision problems a deterministic algorithm solves in polynomial time (at most about n^k steps on an n-bit input, for some fixed k)
ZPP: zero-error probabilistic polynomial time: always correct, expected polynomial time
RP: randomised polynomial time with one-sided error: never accepts a no-instance, accepts each yes-instance with probability at least 1/2
BPP: bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time: decision problems a randomised polynomial-time algorithm answers correctly with probability at least 2/3 on every input
NP: the class NP (nondeterministic polynomial time): decision problems whose yes-answers have a short certificate checkable in polynomial time
PSPACE: decision problems solvable with a polynomial amount of memory, however long it takes
Σ₂: the second level of the polynomial hierarchy: problems of the form "there exists y such that for all z, a polynomial-time check R(x, y, z) holds", with y and z of polynomial length
Π₂: the mirror image of Σ₂: "for all y there exists z" (the complements of Σ₂ problems)
∩: intersection: the problems in both classes
P/poly: problems solvable by polynomial-size circuits, one circuit per input length (equivalently, polynomial time with a polynomial-length advice string that depends only on the input length)
⊆: "is contained in": every problem in the left class is also in the right class (the two may turn out to be equal)
In words: zero-error and one-sided classes sit inside bounded two-sided randomness. RP specifically sits inside NP because its accepting runs cannot be false positives. BPP fits inside polynomial space, the second level of the polynomial hierarchy and polynomial-size circuits.
```

Why each holds:

- **The chain and RP inside NP.** A zero-error algorithm can be cut off and made one-sided; one-sided error is a special case of two-sided. For RP, an accepting coin sequence is a certificate, since no coin sequence makes it accept a no-instance.
- **BPP inside PSPACE.** Try every coin sequence one after another, count acceptances and reuse the space.
- **BPP inside Σ₂ ∩ Π₂** (Sipser, Gács and Lautemann, 1983). So if P equals NP, the whole polynomial hierarchy collapses to P and P equals BPP.
- **BPP inside P/poly**, explained in the advice-string unit. Adleman (1978) proved it for one-sided error (RP); Bennett and Gill (1981) extended it to BPP, and the result is often called Adleman's theorem. The coin string it finds is non-uniform advice, not a known efficient way to find it.

## Key takeaways

- RP is in NP because an accepting random string is a certificate.
- BPP is in PSPACE and in the second level of the polynomial hierarchy.
- BPP being contained in NP is still open.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Randomised complexity — Arora lecture notes](https://users.cs.duke.edu/~reif/courses/complectures/Arora/lec6.pdf)

questions.prompt: Suppose someone proves P equals NP. Using the Sipser–Gács–Lautemann theorem (BPP lies inside the second level of the polynomial hierarchy), what follows about randomised computation?

options.text: Nothing; BPP is unrelated to NP
options.explanation: Through the polynomial hierarchy they're closely linked.

options.text: P equals BPP
options.explanation: Correct. If P equals NP, the whole polynomial hierarchy collapses to P, including its second level. BPP lies inside that level, so BPP equals P.

options.text: BPP equals PSPACE
options.explanation: P equalling NP doesn't collapse PSPACE. P equalling PSPACE would need a separate proof.

options.text: BQP equals P
options.explanation: BQP isn't known to lie inside the polynomial hierarchy (and relative to an oracle it doesn't), so P equalling NP doesn't obviously affect it.

questions.workedExample: The given theorem puts BPP in the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. If P equals NP, both existential and universal polynomially bounded certificate checks collapse to P, level by level. BPP is then inside P; the reverse inclusion already holds. This argument does not collapse PSPACE or BQP.

lessons.title: Advice strings and derandomisation
lessons.summary: A union bound proves one random string works on every input of a fixed length.
lessons.body:
BPP has a polynomial-time randomised decision algorithm correct with probability at least two thirds on each input. Independent majority repetition can make its per-input error exponentially small. Advice allows a different helper string for each input length, unlike a single uniform algorithm.

Adleman's argument first amplifies the error below 2 to the power −n for inputs of n bits, then applies a **union bound** (the chance that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their chances):

```formula essential
Pr[some x fails] ≤ 2^n ε
Pr[some x fails] < 2^n × 2^{−n} = 1
where
x: one of the possible inputs of length n
n: the input length, in bits
2^n: the number of different inputs of length n
ε: the error probability for each single input after amplification, below 2^{−n}
Pr[some x fails]: the probability that a random coin string gives a wrong answer on at least one input of length n
≤, <: is at most, is less than
In words: if every input fails on less than a 2 to the power −n share of coin strings, then fewer than all coin strings fail on any input, so at least one coin string is right on every input of that length. That string becomes the advice.
```

The advice string has polynomial length because the amplified algorithm uses only polynomially many random bits. The proof gives existence separately for each input length; it supplies no efficient way to find the strings.

Open, and surprising: whether BPP is contained in NP. Nobody has proved that randomised algorithms can be simulated by short certificates.

Conjectured: P equals BPP. Impagliazzo and Wigderson (1997) proved a conditional version:

```formula reference
L ∈ E  and  size(L) = 2^{Ω(n)}
  gives  P = BPP
where
L: some decision problem
E: the class of problems solvable in time 2^{O(n)}, exponential with a linear exponent
∈: "is a member of"
size(L): the smallest number of gates in Boolean circuits deciding L on inputs of n bits
n: the input length, in bits
O(n): Big O: at most a constant times n, for large n
Ω(n): Big Omega: at least a constant times n, for large n
P: the complexity class P: decision problems a deterministic algorithm solves in polynomial time (at most about n^k steps on an n-bit input, for some fixed k)
BPP: bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time: decision problems a randomised polynomial-time algorithm answers correctly with probability at least 2/3 on every input
In words: if a problem computable in time exponential in input length requires circuits of size exponential in that length, then every bounded-error randomised polynomial-time decision algorithm has a deterministic polynomial-time replacement.
```

The hypothesis is an unproven circuit lower bound, so the result is conditional. Under this hardness assumption, every BPP decision problem has a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm; the proof does not promise the same exponent or a practical implementation. The primality story fits that pattern.

> [!note] What "P equals BPP" would and wouldn't mean
> It wouldn't make randomness useless: randomised algorithms are often simpler or faster by a polynomial factor, and randomness is essential in cryptography, distributed protocols and sampling. It would mean randomness can't turn exponential into polynomial for decision problems.

## Key takeaways

- A union bound proves one random string works on every input of a fixed length.
- The string is non-uniform advice, with no efficient finding algorithm supplied.
- Strong circuit lower bounds would imply P equals BPP.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Randomised complexity — Arora lecture notes](https://users.cs.duke.edu/~reif/courses/complectures/Arora/lec6.pdf)

options.text: A non-uniform advice string exists; finding it efficiently has not been shown
options.explanation: Correct. The proof supplies a polynomial-size string for each length, but is not an efficient construction.

lessons.title: Qubits, interference and BQP
lessons.summary: A pure qubit register is described by amplitudes, while measurement yields one outcome.
lessons.body:
## Quantum: BQP

A quantum computer on a register of qubits has a pure state described by complex **amplitudes**, one per possible bit string. Quantum gates apply structured linear transformations to that state, and measurement returns a single outcome:

```formula essential
N_amp = 2^n
Pr[x] = |α_x|^2
where
N_amp: the number of entries in the general pure-state amplitude vector; some special states have shorter descriptions
n: the number of qubits
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together: one amplitude per n-bit string
x: one possible measurement outcome, an n-bit string
α_x: alpha sub x, the amplitude (a complex number) attached to outcome x
|α_x|: the magnitude (size) of that complex number
Pr[x]: the probability that measuring the register gives outcome x; these probabilities add up to 1
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a general pure register has one amplitude per possible output bit string, but measurement yields only one string. Its probability is the squared magnitude of that string’s amplitude.
```

The power isn't "trying everything in parallel"; measurement gives you one outcome. It is **quantum interference**: arranging for amplitudes of wrong answers to cancel and right answers to reinforce.

**BQP** is the set of decision problems solvable by a polynomial-time-uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits with error at most 1/3 (amplifiable, as for BPP).

What's proven:

```formula essential
P ⊆ BPP ⊆ BQP ⊆ PP ⊆ PSPACE
where
P: the complexity class P: decision problems a deterministic algorithm solves in polynomial time (at most about n^k steps on an n-bit input, for some fixed k)
BPP: bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time: decision problems a randomised polynomial-time algorithm answers correctly with probability at least 2/3 on every input
BQP: bounded-error quantum polynomial time: decision problems a quantum computer solves in polynomial time with error at most 1/3 on every input
PP: probabilistic polynomial time: yes-instances are accepted with probability greater than one half, while no-instances are accepted with probability at most one half. There is no fixed success gap as in BPP, so the usual polynomial-repetition amplification guarantee does not follow
PSPACE: decision problems solvable with a polynomial amount of memory, however long it takes
⊆: "is contained in": every problem in the left class is also in the right class (the two may turn out to be equal)
In words: everything a classical randomised computer can do efficiently, a quantum computer can too, and everything a quantum computer can do efficiently fits inside PP and inside polynomial space.
```

- BQP inside PSPACE (Bernstein and Vazirani, 1993): sum the amplitudes path by path, reusing space.
- BQP inside PP (Adleman, DeMarrais and Huang, 1997).

Since BPP sits inside BQP and BQP inside PSPACE, separating BQP from BPP would also separate BPP from PSPACE. Because P sits inside BPP, it would also separate P from PSPACE.

So proving BQP and BPP different would prove P and PSPACE different, which is far beyond current techniques. This rules out claiming a proven separation of BQP from BPP. It does not rule out proven query-complexity advantages or smaller speed-ups within polynomial time.

## Key takeaways

- A pure qubit register is described by amplitudes, while measurement yields one outcome.
- BPP is contained in BQP, PP and PSPACE.
- Separating BPP from BQP would also separate P from PSPACE.

## Further reading

- [Computational Complexity — Arora and Barak](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/book.pdf)
- [Randomised complexity — Arora lecture notes](https://users.cs.duke.edu/~reif/courses/complectures/Arora/lec6.pdf)

questions.prompt: Why has nobody proved that BQP and BPP are different classes, even though Shor's algorithm factors in quantum polynomial time and no fast classical factoring algorithm is known?

options.text: Because factoring might be NP-complete
options.explanation: Whether factoring is NP-complete has no bearing on this; and it is believed not to be.

options.text: Because BQP lies inside PSPACE, so separating BQP from BPP would separate BPP, and hence P, from PSPACE: far beyond current techniques
options.explanation: Separating polynomial-time quantum decision computation from all polynomial-time classical randomised computation would separate P from PSPACE. This does not exclude query-model or within-polynomial speed-ups.

options.text: Because Shor's algorithm hasn't been run on large numbers
options.explanation: Experiments can't prove complexity separations; this is a mathematical barrier, not an engineering one.

options.text: Because BQP and BPP have been proved equal
options.explanation: It hasn't; it's open, and most experts believe BQP is strictly larger.

questions.workedExample: BPP is contained in BQP, which is contained in PSPACE. If some BQP problem were outside BPP, PSPACE would also contain a problem outside BPP and therefore outside P. That would separate P from PSPACE, a major open problem. Shor’s algorithm is an upper bound; lack of a known fast classical factoring algorithm is not a lower-bound proof.

lessons.title: Shor, Grover and the limits of quantum evidence
lessons.summary: Shor gives quantum polynomial-time factoring and discrete logarithms.
lessons.body:
BQP contains decision problems solved with bounded error by uniform polynomial-size quantum circuits. Factoring and search also have function versions, where the algorithm returns a factorisation or an item. Use the associated decision version when placing them in a decision complexity class.

### Shor and Grover

- **Shor (1994)** factors integers and computes discrete logarithms in polynomial time on a quantum computer. The associated factoring decision problem is in BQP; Shor also recovers the factors. It is **not known** to be outside BPP; the leading general-purpose classical method (the general number field sieve) has a heuristic expected subexponential-time analysis. This breaks RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography once large fault-tolerant machines exist, which is why NIST standardised post-quantum schemes such as ML-KEM (FIPS 203) in 2024. Algorithmic polynomial time does not establish that a sufficiently large fault-tolerant machine is available.
- **Grover (1996)** searches unstructured items with about the square root of the number of queries a classical search needs (below). This is **proven optimal** for black-box search (Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani, 1997). For brute-force SAT it is a quadratic speed-up, still exponential.

```formula essential
Q ≈ (π/4) × √N
N = 2^n  gives  √N = 2^{n/2}
where
Q: the number of queries (evaluations of the black-box function) Grover's algorithm makes
N: the number of possible items to search, with exactly one marked item for the approximate leading constant
π: pi, about 3.14159, so π/4 ≈ 0.785
√N: the square root of the candidate count
n: the number of bits (or Boolean variables) being searched over, so there are 2^n candidates
≈: approximately equal to
In words: quantum black-box search uses a square-root number of queries compared with the candidate count. For all assignments to Boolean variables, the count is exponential; taking its square root reduces the exponent but leaves exponential growth.
```

> [!warning] Quantum computers are not believed to solve NP-complete problems efficiently
> Factoring is in both NP and coNP and not believed NP-complete. Grover's bound shows that any quantum algorithm treating SAT as a black box needs about the square root of the 2-to-the-n brute-force steps (n variables). Whether NP is contained in BQP is open, but it is widely believed false.

### Evidence about BQP

- **Oracle separations**: Raz and Tal (2018) found an oracle relative to which BQP is not contained in the polynomial hierarchy. This is evidence, not proof, about the real world (use the earlier relativisation barrier).
- **Quantum advantage experiments**: Google's 2019 random-circuit sampling claim targeted a *sampling* task believed hard classically under complexity assumptions. Improved classical simulations later narrowed the claimed gap. Such experiments test conjectures; they don't prove separations.

## The map, with confidence levels

| Relationship | Status |
|---|---|
| P inside BPP inside BQP inside PSPACE | Proven |
| BPP inside Σ₂ and Π₂ | Proven |
| P equals BPP | Conjectured |
| BPP inside NP | Open |
| Factoring in BQP | Proven (Shor) |
| Factoring not in BPP | Believed, unproven |
| NP inside BQP | Believed false |

The Grover estimate assumes one marked item, ideal coherent oracle access and a sufficiently large search space. With multiple solutions the query count depends on how many are marked; with none, a search procedure needs an appropriate existence test. Cipher evaluations here mean reversible quantum oracle queries, not equal-cost classical CPU operations. Doubling a symmetric key length restores the generic query exponent in this model; physical costs, parallelism and nongeneric cryptanalysis need separate analysis.

## Key takeaways

- Shor gives quantum polynomial-time factoring and discrete logarithms.
- Grover’s square-root black-box speed-up remains exponential for assignment search.
- Oracle and sampling evidence do not prove an unrelativised decision-class separation.

## Further reading

- [Shor’s factoring algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9508027)
- [Grover’s search algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9605043)
- [Dated RSA resource estimate — Gidney, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15917)
- [ML-KEM standard — NIST](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/203/final)
